scriptTemplate.title: FAM4701 Script

studyNotes.headline: Discussion items

items.text: OCF is a stalled or departed condition where normal control inputs may be ineffective or even make the departure worse. The study goal is to recognize it early, stop improvising, and execute the published recovery without chasing sensations.

children.text: Poststall gyrations show rapid uncommanded motions, erratic airspeed, stalled AOA, and a turn needle that may fluctuate instead of staying pegged.
Incipient spin is the transition between gyrations and a steady spin. Expect oscillatory spin-like motion, a fully pegged turn needle, stalled AOA, and airspeed moving toward the steady-spin range.
Steady-state spin usually shows pegged stalled AOA, a pegged turn needle, and about 120 to 135 KIAS with roughly 400 to 500 feet of altitude loss per turn.
AOA helps tell you whether the aircraft is still stalled: about 18 or more units in an erect spin, near 0 units in an inverted spin.
A rapidly increasing airspeed with a pegged turn needle points toward a spiral, not a true spin.
Use the altimeter to manage time and decide whether there is enough altitude left to finish the recovery.

items.text: What the instruments are really telling you:

children.text: Set PCL to IDLE.
Place the controls physically neutral and visually confirm the stick, rudder, and elevator are centered.
Check altitude, then recover from the resulting unusual attitude once the aircraft starts flying again.
If the aircraft is not recovering, slowly feed forward stick until the elevator reaches neutral and the nose breaks free.
A spin stays stalled, normally lives in the 120 to 135 KIAS range, and can often be stabilized by neutral controls.
A spiral is not stalled, the airspeed will keep increasing, and anti-spin inputs are not the fix. Keep PCL at IDLE, stay patient, and wait for normal control response before you recover.
Time distortion makes the departure feel much slower than it is. Pilots tend to change inputs too soon or cycle the controls if they do not trust the procedure.
G cues can be misleading, especially in an eyeballs-out condition. Do not fly the recovery by feel.
Holding elevator aft of neutral can stop the recovery entirely.
Premature anti-spin or control cycling only delays recovery.
Power-on or inverted departures can overstress the engine, so even a successful recovery usually drives a land-as-soon-as-practical decision.
Recovery from unusual attitudes and aerobatics is expected by 6000 feet AGL.
If the aircraft is still in an unrecoverable rapid descent below 6000 feet AGL, the answer is uncontrolled ejection.

items.text: Contact unusual-attitude recovery is a visual recovery tool for a controlled aircraft. If the aircraft is stalled, departing, or you are unsure which branch you are in, stop trying to salvage it and transition to OCF recovery.

children.text: Set PCL to MAX when the airspeed is low.
Roll past 90 degrees of bank toward the nearest horizon and use positive back-stick to bring the nose down.
If needed, let the rollout wait until the nose is clearly below the horizon so you can regain enough airspeed to feel the controls again.
Common errors are not taking MAX power when the aircraft is slow, trying to push the nose over with forward stick, or stopping the roll with the nose still high.
Roll to the nearest horizon while simultaneously retarding PCL to IDLE.
Use speed brake as required and keep the pull smooth so you do not trade the dive for an accelerated stall.
Do not let the recovery exceed 316 KIAS, and be ready to perform AGSM as the pull builds.
If the aircraft is not responding normally and the AOA picture says you are stalled, execute OCF recovery instead of forcing the pull.
Roll in the shortest direction to place the aircraft upright, then use power as required once the nose is on or slightly above the horizon.
Check and report oil pressure as the aircraft comes back upright.
Common errors are choosing the long way around or adding unnecessary pitch while still inverted.
Unusual-attitude recovery is expected to be complete by 6000 feet AGL.
Airspeed and nose position alone do not guarantee the wing is unstalled; AOA lag and pitch bucking are why you stay alert for an accelerated stall developing underneath the recovery.

items.text: An aileron roll is a 360-degree roll about the longitudinal axis. The nose traces a small circle around the horizon and the aircraft should finish on the entry heading with the energy picture still under control.

children.text: Set up 180 to 220 KIAS with about 80 percent PCL, complete the Pre-Stalling, Spinning, and Aerobatic Checklist, and clear the area onto a good section line.
Raise the nose to about 10 degrees nose high, relax the back-stick pressure so the nose stops tracking upward, then apply brisk aileron in the desired direction.
As the aircraft approaches wings level, neutralize the aileron and return to level flight.
The aircraft is wings level, near the entry altitude, and back on the original heading without the nose dropping through the inverted portion.
The classic error is holding back-stick during the roll, which turns the maneuver into an arcing barrel-looking roll and drives the nose down rapidly while inverted.
Delaying the roll once the nose-high picture is set lets the airspeed bleed off and makes the roll sluggish.

items.text: A loop is a 360-degree turn in the vertical plane flown on a constant heading and nose track. It is the foundation for most of the later vertical maneuvers, so the goal is a smooth pitch rate, balanced flight, and a recovery back on the entry line.

children.text: Set up 230 to 250 KIAS with PCL at MAX, complete PSSA, clear the working area, and check and report the entry altitude over ICS before the pull.
Begin AGSM and pull smoothly to about 4 G in 2 to 3 seconds with no aileron input.
As airspeed slows, use increasing right rudder to stay balanced and keep the wings parallel to the horizon with only small aileron corrections.
Expect about 100 to 120 KIAS over the top, then fly the nose back down the section line and recover with about 4 G while resuming AGSM.
You recover wings level on the original heading and back near the altitude where you started.
If the airspeed is below 180 KIAS before the nose reaches vertical in the first quarter, terminate with a nose-high unusual-attitude recovery.
If the aircraft becomes stalled or excessively slow, go straight to OCF recovery, then add power only after oil pressure is normal and AOA is back below 18 units.

items.text: A half Cuban eight is the front side of a loop followed by a half roll from a 45-degree nose-low inverted picture. It should finish on the reciprocal heading at the original altitude with the 45-degree down line fully under control before the pullout starts.

children.text: Set up 230 to 250 KIAS with PCL at MAX, complete PSSA, clear the area, and start with enough altitude to budget roughly 3000 feet through the maneuver.
Pull like the front half of a loop with about 4 G while keeping the aircraft balanced and the wings parallel to the horizon.
As the nose falls toward the 45-degree nose-low inverted picture, freeze the stick momentarily, execute the coordinated half roll, and use slight forward stick through the roll to hold the down line.
Keep the 45-degree nose-low picture stable and start the pullout around 205 to 210 KIAS.
The aircraft recovers level at the original altitude, on reciprocal heading, and near the entry energy.
Most misses come from carrying the front half like a poor loop, then adding aft stick during the half roll or raising the nose too early after the roll is finished.
Use a ground reference or heading aid to keep the 45-degree down line honest instead of guessing at it.

items.text: An Immelmann is a half loop followed by a half roll to upright. It trades airspeed for altitude and direction reversal, so the important picture is a smooth climb to the reciprocal horizon and a disciplined roll timing at the top.

children.text: Set up 230 to 250 KIAS with PCL at MAX, complete PSSA, clear the area, and report entry altitude before starting the pull.
Start with AGSM and pull about 4 G in 2 to 3 seconds, keeping the stick centered laterally and adding right rudder as the airspeed decays.

As the nose approaches about 10 degrees above the opposite horizon, relax the back-stick, execute the half roll to upright, and use only the small amount of forward stick needed to keep the nose from falling through.
The aircraft is wings level on the reciprocal heading, slightly nose high, and still flying with usable energy rather than dropping away from the horizon.
The common misses are poor rudder discipline in the pull, initiating the half roll too early or too late, and letting the nose drop after rolling upright.

items.text: A Split-S combines a half roll to inverted with the back side of a loop. It is a rapid direction reversal that turns altitude into airspeed, so it only works if the inverted setup is clean before the pull starts.

children.text: Transition to 150 KIAS, retard PCL to IDLE, maintain altitude while slowing to about 140 KIAS, raise the nose to about 10 degrees, and complete PSSA with a clear section line.
Roll the aircraft to wings-level inverted, verify the wings are actually level against the horizon, then apply back-stick to bring the nose through without stalling.
As airspeed and G build, expect about 4 G in the pullout and perform AGSM.
Once back level, check and report normal oil pressure, then add power as required.
The aircraft is back in level flight on the reciprocal heading with normal oil pressure and the pull has stayed controlled instead of becoming an accelerated stall.
If the aircraft does not respond normally once the pull starts, stop trying to muscle it through and execute OCF recovery.
Student solos are prohibited from Split-S, Immelmann, Combination Maneuver, and intentional sustained inverted flight.

items.text: A wingover is a 180-degree reversal built from a smooth climbing turn followed by a smooth diving turn. It is a finesse maneuver, not a max-performance pull, and it should be flown in a two-leaf series that returns you to the original heading.

children.text: Set up 200 to 220 KIAS with about 70 percent PCL, complete PSSA, clear the area, and place a good reference point directly off a wingtip.
Blend elevator, rudder, and aileron together so the aircraft reaches about 45 degrees nose high and 45 degrees of bank halfway through the turn.
Continue the turn so that the aircraft reaches about 90 degrees of bank with the nose on the horizon at 90 degrees of turn, then let the nose fall and roll out symmetrically.

At about 135 degrees of turn you should see roughly 45 degrees of bank and about 35 degrees nose low before the aircraft comes back to the horizon. Then immediately begin the second leaf in the opposite direction.
The second wingover recovers wings level on the original heading, original altitude, and about the original airspeed.
Rushing the maneuver, missing the 45-up/45-bank picture, or starting the second leaf off airspeed are the normal ways to make a wingover ugly.
A long road or section line is a great outside reference because the two turns should look like the curved portion of a dollar sign.

items.text: A barrel roll is a 360-degree roll around an imaginary point about 45 degrees off the nose. The outside picture should feel like the aircraft is corkscrewing around that point, not simply rolling in place.

children.text: Set up 200 to 220 KIAS with about 80 percent PCL, complete PSSA, clear the area, and pick the 45-degree reference point before you move the nose.
Raise the nose smoothly with wings level. As the nose passes about 20 degrees above the horizon, begin the coordinated roll-and-pull.

At about 45 degrees of turn you should see roughly 90 degrees of bank and 55 to 60 degrees nose high, then reach wings-level inverted at the 90-degree checkpoint with about 100 to 120 KIAS and the nose still around 10 degrees above the horizon.
Hold a positive G feel throughout and let the backside mirror the front side so the aircraft finishes on the original heading and altitude.
The aircraft recovers on the original heading and altitude with a symmetric arc above and below the horizon.
Do not exceed about 2.5 G during the maneuver.
The most common misses are failing to raise the nose enough in the first 45 degrees, letting the roll rate accelerate through inverted, or not driving the nose low enough on the backside.

items.text: A combination maneuver is a planned sequence of up to four aerobatic maneuvers flown as one continuous evolution. The grading focus is less about any single maneuver and more about whether you stay ahead of the aircraft while preserving orientation and energy.

children.text: Choose the sequence before takeoff, brief the order with the IP, and build the plan around realistic altitude and energy transitions instead of wishful thinking.
Fly the first maneuver cleanly, but start thinking about the next picture before the current one is finished.
Sequence higher-energy maneuvers before lower-energy ones so you are not trying to invent extra airspeed or altitude in the middle of the chain.
The full sequence ends on the planned heading, within the working area, and without an obvious energy or orientation surprise between maneuvers.
Late planning is the usual killer. Students finish one maneuver, realize the next setup is wrong, and then spend the rest of the sequence improvising.

items.text: Inverted flight is intentional, wings-level inverted flight flown for no more than the published time limit. The maneuver is really an exercise in outside references, restraint discipline, and oil-pressure awareness.

children.text: Set up 180 to 200 KIAS, complete PSSA, clear the area, and tighten the restraint harness before the roll.
Raise the nose about 10 degrees, relax the back-stick so the nose stops climbing, and roll smoothly to wings-level inverted.
Apply the forward stick needed to hold altitude, note the clock immediately, and check oil pressure as soon as you are stable.
Use the proper outside reference to stay level, then roll upright with coordinated controls before the time or oil-pressure limits are challenged.
The aircraft is upright again with normal oil pressure and no more than 60 seconds spent inverted.
The usual misses are poor restraint setup, sloppy level-flight references while inverted, and staying inverted too long because the clock check was late.

events.overview: This event turns the spin family into distinct problems instead of one big emergency blob. You should be ready to brief a clean erect spin entry and recovery, recognize when an inverted or progressive spin is actually developing, and then switch gears to accelerated-stall cues and a disciplined AOA approach picture.

notes: Adjust specifics to match the assigned profile, weather, and local procedures.
Because the blocks are shared, one edit updates every event that references the same procedure or comm call.
scriptTemplate.title: FAM4702 Script

studyNotes.headline: Discussion items

items.text: The intentional erect spin teaches you how a fully stalled, yaw-driven departure is entered, recognized, and recovered before altitude discipline becomes the real emergency. The point is not to be dramatic; it is to make the recovery inputs feel procedural instead of surprising.

children.text: Trim the aircraft for about 150 KIAS in straight-and-level flight, complete PSSA, clear the area, and do not enter below 13,500 feet AGL.
The overall event guardrails still matter: enter below 22,000 feet PA and be recovered above 10,000 feet PA.
Retard PCL to IDLE first, then raise the nose to about 30 degrees nose high.
At the first stick shaker, add slight rudder in the desired spin direction.
At the full stall and nose drop, apply full rudder in the direction of rotation, full aft stick, and keep the ailerons neutral.
Call out altitude, AOA, airspeed, and turn-needle indications so you stay ahead of what the aircraft is doing.
Recover with the published Inadvertent Departure from Controlled Flight procedure rather than trying to create a private spin technique.
Once the rotation stops, neutralize the rudder and recover from the resulting unusual attitude without pulling so aggressively that you create a secondary stall.
After recovery, check and report oil pressure before you add power back in.

Common misses are raising the nose before PCL is at IDLE, letting external fixation delay the recovery, forgetting to neutralize controls as the rotation stops, or pulling too hard in the recovery and stalling it again.
Ailerons stay neutral in the spin, and aft stick held at the wrong time can delay recovery.

items.text: Intentional inverted spins are prohibited. You still need to understand them because a poorly managed inverted departure can flatten into an unusual picture that looks very different from an erect spin.

children.text: The usual setup is a high-pitch, high-power, low-airspeed mistake: roughly 60 to 90 degrees nose high, PCL at MAX, and around 50 KIAS before the aircraft rolls and departs.
Torque and aft-CG effects drive the departure more than the clean yaw entry picture you use for an erect spin.
Expect a flatter spin than the erect case, often around 30 degrees nose low with slight pitch oscillations.
Airspeed is typically around 40 KIAS, AOA trends toward 0 units, and the G cue is negative, around minus 1.5 G.
If the nose is steeply down and the airspeed is rapidly increasing, you may actually be looking at an inverted spiral instead.
An early reduction of PCL to IDLE is the first high-value move because power helps sustain the inverted spin.
With PCL at IDLE and ailerons neutral, some incipient inverted departures will transition out of the spin or become an inverted spiral that you then sort out with the published OCF logic.
Do not confuse a steep, accelerating inverted spiral with the flatter low-airspeed inverted spin picture.
Leaving power at MAX is exactly how you keep the inverted spin going.
Speed-brake position is not the magic answer here; it is not what decides whether the departure develops or recovers.

items.text: A progressive spin is not a new maneuver. It is what you create by applying the wrong recovery inputs to a steady-state spin, which is why this brief is really about avoiding self-inflicted escalation.

children.text: The classic cause is reversing rudder while still holding full aft stick during a steady-state spin recovery attempt.
That combination drops the nose, keeps the aircraft rotating in the original direction for roughly 1.5 to 2 more turns, and drives the airspeed up hard.
Airspeed can build as high as about 175 KIAS while the aircraft is still rotating, which is one reason the sight picture feels worse than a normal spin.
If the wrong rudder and aft stick are held long enough, the aircraft can settle into a steady-state spin in the opposite direction.
Do not try to invent a special progressive-spin technique. Go back to the published OCF/departure recovery procedure and stop the control-input mistake that caused the problem.
The real prevention is procedural discipline: identify the direction of rotation, apply the correct rudder logic once, and do not reverse it because the airplane feels wrong.

items.text: An accelerated stall is a stall driven by excessive AOA under load, not by slow indicated airspeed alone. It is the trap that catches pilots who think a fast airplane cannot still be stalled if they are pulling hard enough.

children.text: The event emphasis is the approach-turn and abrupt-pull environment, but the core lesson is broader: a wing stalls whenever you demand more lift than it can produce.
Higher bank angle means higher load factor, which means higher stall speed and less margin if you keep pulling.
Expect more pronounced buffet once you get above about 2 G, with especially heavy buffet above about 3 G.
The break is often an abrupt lateral roll-off rather than a gentle nose-drop warning.
At 90 degrees of bank the lift requirement becomes impossible, which is why the aircraft simply falls if you try to hold it there.
Reduce AOA first by easing the back-stick and unloading the wing.
Reduce bank angle as required, then rebuild airspeed instead of trying to hold the same turn and make the buffet go away.
Do not sustain heavy buffet in an attempt to salvage the maneuver; that only adds overstress risk.
The common mental trap is focusing on IAS and ignoring that a hard pull at 200 KIAS can still exceed critical AOA.
This is one more reason nose-low unusual-attitude recoveries must stay smooth. An aggressive pull can turn the recovery itself into the stall.

items.text: The AOA approach teaches you to fly the aircraft at the optimum on-speed condition instead of chasing one fixed airspeed. The scan is simple on purpose: keep the aircraft at about 10.5 units AOA, control rate of descent with power, and still transition to a normal flared landing.

children.text: After a touch-and-go, climb out at 120 KIAS with flaps up and return to pattern altitude.
On downwind, reduce power to about 15 to 20 percent, configure as briefed, and transition to the amber-donut on-speed picture.
Approximate on-speed references are about 110 KIAS flaps up, 100 KIAS flaps TO, and 95 KIAS flaps LDG, but the real target is 10 to 11 units AOA regardless of weight or flap setting.
Once on speed, use about 25 to 30 percent power to hold pattern altitude and keep 3/4 to 1 wingtip spacing on downwind.
Complete the Before Landing Checklist before abeam.
At the 180, reduce power back toward 15 to 20 percent, lower the nose slightly to hold 10.5 units, and start the turn.
Expect less bank than a normal pattern, especially with TO or LDG flaps, so you do not tighten the turn unnecessarily.
At the 90, the target is still 10.5 units and about 450 feet AGL.
On final, scan the AOA indexer, aim point, and altimeter together. Use pitch to keep the donut and power to manage the glidepath.
When established with about 1200 to 1500 feet of straightaway remaining, you want about 200 feet AGL and 10.5 units until you are beyond the runway numbers.
This is still an AOA approach to a normal flared landing, not an AOA arrival all the way onto the runway. Expect to add power during the flare transition as the nose lowers.
Flaps-up AOA approaches are difficult and can create high descent rates at low power, so flaps LDG is preferred and flaps TO is only a compromise.
The biggest misses are over-correcting nose attitude, forgetting that power changes affect the AOA picture, using normal-pattern bank angles, and failing to transition to a normal flare.

studyNotes.summary: Keep the spin branches separate in your head, then brief the accelerated-stall and AOA patterns with the same level of discipline.

events.overview: This event is about understanding what the airplane can structurally tolerate before you ask it to recover. Be ready to explain how the Vn diagram drives maneuvering-speed decisions, why abrupt or multi-axis inputs can still overstress the aircraft, and how to brief an emergency procedure all the way from recognition to landing or ejection logic.

notes: Adjust specifics to match the assigned profile, weather, and local procedures.
Because the blocks are shared, one edit updates every event that references the same procedure or comm call.
scriptTemplate.title: FAM4703 Script

studyNotes.headline: Discussion items

items.text: The T-6B Vn diagram is the picture that ties airspeed, load factor, stall margin, and structural limits together. If you understand this diagram, accelerated stalls and overstress are no longer separate topics; they are just different ways to leave the safe part of the envelope.

children.text: The left side of the diagram is the stall boundary, where the wing simply cannot produce the lift you are demanding.
The upper and lower boundaries are structural load limits, where the airplane may still be flying but the airframe is no longer being treated kindly.
Flap configuration changes the available lift and stall speed, but it does not make the airplane structurally invincible.

items.text: What the diagram is showing you:

children.text: Low airspeed is not required for a stall. A hard pull at high airspeed can still drive the wing past critical AOA.
The FTI example is worth remembering: a sharp pull at about 200 KIAS can produce an accelerated stall around the 5 G region even though the 1 G stall speed is much lower.
That is why steep turns, downhill recoveries, and panicked pullouts deserve the same respect as obvious slow-flight stall setups.
Know where stall, overstress, and maneuvering-speed logic meet on the same graph.
Be able to explain why load factor increases stall speed and why the answer to an accelerated stall is unloading the wing, not pulling harder.

items.text: Maneuvering speed is the highest airspeed at which a full control deflection in one axis should stall the airplane before it structurally overstresses it. It is not permission to make violent multi-axis inputs and assume the airplane will sort itself out.

children.text: VO is 227 KIAS.
Above VO, a full or abrupt control input in one axis can cause structural damage before the aircraft stalls.
Full rudder above 150 KIAS exceeds rudder system limits even if you are still below VO.
Below VO, the protection only applies to one-axis full deflection. It is not a blanket shield against every abrupt control combination.

Use maneuvering speed as a control-discipline reminder during aerobatics, unusual-attitude recoveries, and any downhill acceleration where you may be tempted to snatch the airplane back to the horizon.
The rudder limit matters because startled feet at higher airspeeds can damage the aircraft long before the rest of the recovery looks obviously bad.
Students often memorize 227 KIAS but forget the one-axis condition that makes the rule true.
The other common miss is treating rudder like a free control at any airspeed. It is not.

items.text: Acceleration limitations are the practical extension of the Vn diagram. They answer the question: what actually bends the airplane when the workload spikes?

children.text: Abrupt full control movement in more than one axis can overstress the aircraft even below VO.
Heavy buffet and rapidly building G are warnings to unload and re-sort, not signs that you should keep pulling until the airplane obeys.
Any high-speed recovery should be flown smoothly enough that you stay ahead of airspeed, G, and rudder limitations together.
Accelerated stalls often begin when a pilot tries to save altitude with a hard pull instead of reducing AOA.
A nose-low recovery, spin recovery pullout, or aerobatic downhill segment can all become acceleration-limit problems if the control inputs are abrupt.
The correct mindset is smooth unload, controlled re-entry into the safe envelope, then rebuild the picture instead of forcing it all at once.
Be able to connect acceleration limits back to maneuvering speed and the Vn diagram rather than briefing them as isolated trivia.
If the explanation never mentions load factor, AOA, and control-input smoothness, it is too shallow.

items.text: Treat this as a cumulative oral spot check. The instructor may choose any emergency procedure and expect you to brief it from recognition through the decision branch that ends in continuation, landing, forced landing, or ejection.

children.text: Start with the recognition cue, then the memory items, then the associated N/W/Cs. Do not jump straight to rote steps.

After the immediate action, be ready to explain what changes the plan: altitude, controllability, engine response, field options, and whether the problem is becoming a PEL, forced-landing, or ejection scenario.
If the EP is critical-action, know the first actions cold enough that you are not using the checklist as a first-look crutch.

Representative study set: Fire on Ground, Emergency Engine Shutdown on the Ground, Emergency Ground Egress, CFS and Ejection CRM, Abort Takeoff, Aircraft Departs Prepared Surface, Engine Failure Immediately After Takeoff, Engine Failure During Flight, Immediate Air-Start, PMU NORM Air-Start, PMU OFF Air-Start, and Uncommanded Power Changes/LOP.
Your goal is not to memorize one instructor's favorite EP list. It is to show that any previously taught FAM emergency can be briefed cleanly and accurately.
If you can only recite steps but cannot explain when to land immediately, continue to a field, or eject, you are not actually ready for this question.
Keep the EP language readable and exact. This event should feel like a clean oral-review standard, not like a pile of disconnected memory items.

studyNotes.summary: Understand how flight loads, maneuvering speed, and control inputs interact, then be able to brief any previously taught FAM emergency procedure with real branch logic.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Instrument scan starts with attitude flying: set power and attitude for the desired performance, then scan to detect error early enough that the correction stays small.

children.text: PAT means Power, Attitude, Trim. Power and attitude establish the performance; trim removes the pressure so the scan can stay ahead of the aircraft.
The power/control instruments are the ADI and torque gauge. Use them to set the initial pitch, bank, and power picture.
The crosscheck/performance instruments include altimeter, VSI, airspeed, AOB or roll pointer, turn needle, HSI, and sideslip indicator.
Use the ADI as the hub and the performance instruments as the spokes.
A basic scan sequence is gyro, nose, gyro, wing, gyro, performance or progress, gyro, then additional yaw and power fine-tuning.
Expect the ADI to take about half of the scan. It gives the big picture while the spokes tell you what needs fine tuning.
For straight and level, use altimeter and VSI for nose, HSI for wing, airspeed for performance, and sideslip plus torque for additional checks.
For constant airspeed climbs and descents, airspeed is the nose crosscheck, HSI is the wing crosscheck, and altimeter is the progress instrument.
If the scan only finds large errors, it is too slow. The goal is early error detection and timely correction.

items.text: Airspeed changes teach smooth power changes while holding heading and altitude. The control loop is simple, but the rudder, pitch, and trim changes happen quickly enough to expose a weak scan.

children.text: Practice airspeed changes normally between 150 and 200 KIAS in straight-and-level flight.
Before changing speed, stabilize heading and altitude, then use PAT instead of chasing the airspeed with pitch alone.
For acceleration, advance power to maximum allowable, anticipate right rudder with the power addition, hold altitude with pitch, and trim as pressure builds.
As the aircraft approaches the target airspeed, reduce power as required to hold the new speed and anticipate left rudder with the power reduction.
For deceleration, reduce power to about 15% torque, anticipate left rudder, maintain altitude with pitch, and trim through the change.
Approaching the slower target airspeed, add power as required to maintain the new speed and anticipate right rudder.
The aircraft is back in trimmed, level flight at the assigned heading, altitude, and target airspeed.
The speed brake can help with rapid deceleration, but late retraction can overshoot the target airspeed.
Common errors are heading drift from weak rudder or rudder trim and altitude deviations from a slow crosscheck.

items.text: Steep turns are still instrument turns: set the attitude on the ADI, then use scan discipline to hold altitude, AOB, airspeed, and rollout heading.

children.text: Practice steep turns normally at 45 or 60 degrees AOB and about 150 KIAS.
For 150 KIAS, expect about 45% torque and 3 degrees nose high for 45 degrees AOB, and about 60% torque and 4 degrees nose high for 60 degrees AOB.
Enter like a normal instrument turn, then add power as bank increases to preserve airspeed.
Hold a constant AOB and correct altitude primarily with pitch.
If a 60-degree turn is descending faster than 1000 FPM, momentarily reduce AOB enough to regain the pitch picture.
Use the one-third rollout rule: start rollout about 15 degrees early from 45 degrees AOB and about 20 degrees early from 60 degrees AOB.
The aircraft rolls out on assigned heading, altitude, and airspeed without a balloon or late power correction.
Common errors are altitude loss, drifting away from the assigned AOB, and being late to set the power picture.
Do not fixate on the HSI during rollout; missing the ADI picture usually causes ballooning or a sloppy recovery.

items.text: Timed turns prove whether the scan can hold altitude and airspeed while the aircraft turns at a predictable rate to an assigned heading.

children.text: Start practice turns at 150 KIAS on a cardinal heading.
Lead the clock by 3 seconds before 00 or 30 seconds so the target rate is established on time.
Use a standard-rate turn or 30 degrees AOB, whichever occurs first, when flying in IMC.
For half standard rate, start with about 10% of indicated airspeed as AOB and crosscheck one needle-width deflection.
Half standard rate turns 30 degrees in 20 seconds. Check heading and clock at each 30-degree checkpoint.
For standard rate, start with about 20% of indicated airspeed as AOB and crosscheck two needle-width deflection.
Standard rate turns 30 degrees in 10 seconds. Use the same ahead-or-behind analysis, but scan the nose more aggressively because bank is steeper.
The aircraft rolls out on the assigned heading, on time, with altitude and airspeed still under control.
For half standard rate, correct between about 10 and 20 degrees AOB.
For standard rate, correct between about 15 and 30 degrees AOB.
Common errors are missing the 3-second lead, confusing ahead versus behind, overcorrecting bank, flying unbalanced, or losing altitude from a poor nose attitude.

items.text: Constant airspeed climbs and descents build the habit that nose attitude controls airspeed while power primarily changes climb or descent performance.

children.text: Set a clean aircraft at 150 KIAS on a numbered or cardinal heading.
Crosscheck airspeed for nose, HSI for wing, altimeter for progress, and sideslip plus torque for additional control.
For descent, reduce power to about 15% and lower the nose to 0 degrees, anticipating left rudder.
Adjust nose attitude to hold 150 KIAS.
About 50 feet before level-off, add power to about 33% and raise the nose to about 3.5 degrees nose high, anticipating right rudder.
For climb, add power to about 55% and raise the nose to about 6 degrees nose high, anticipating right rudder.
About 50 feet before level-off from the climb, reduce power to about 33% and lower the nose to about 3.5 degrees nose high, anticipating left rudder.
The aircraft levels at the assigned altitude with 150 KIAS, heading control, and trim stabilized.
Pitch is primarily airspeed control, but pitch changes also affect VSI; power is the main rate-control tool.
Common errors are weak rudder trim, slow power setting, and overcontrolling the nose while correcting airspeed.

items.text: Enroute descent is a controlled high-rate descent that still has to look predictable to ATC and stable in the last 1000 feet before level-off.

children.text: Confirm the assigned altitude, report leaving the current altitude for the new altitude, and start the descent checklist.
Plan the descent so the final 1000 feet can be reduced to a controlled 500 to 1500 FPM instead of arriving at level-off with excess rate.
Establish and maintain about 200 to 250 KIAS and roughly 4000 FPM, then fine tune power and nose attitude as required.
About 1000 feet before level-off, adjust pitch to slow the descent to 500 to 1500 FPM.
Level at the assigned altitude and transition to the desired cruise speed with power as required.
For the NATOPS enroute descent profile, lower the nose about 10 degrees nose low, set about 10% torque approaching 220 KIAS, and fine tune around 220 KIAS and 4000 FPM.
The aircraft is level at the assigned altitude, back in a cruise-speed plan, and no longer carrying a high descent rate.
The speed brake or idle power can create very high descent rates, so use them only with a plan to be stabilized by the last 1000 feet.
Common errors are missing the descent checklist, losing heading with power or airspeed changes, and failing to reduce rate before level-off.

studyNotes.summary: Build the scan first: use PAT to set the performance picture, then use the right crosscheck instrument to catch and correct small errors before they become large deviations.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: IMC emergency discussion starts with control and judgment, not checklist recitation. Stabilize the aircraft, build the instrument scan, then solve the emergency.

children.text: NATOPS emergency procedures are the best available procedures, but they do not replace pilot judgment when weather, terrain, multiple malfunctions, or crew status change the problem.
The basic emergency order is maintain aircraft control, analyze the situation, take proper action, and land as soon as conditions permit.
Critical action or memory items come first when required; time permitting, back them up with the checklist to ensure completeness.
Brief how the answer changes between VMC and IMC. In IMC, altitude, terrain clearance, ATC coordination, and spatial-disorientation risk usually matter before local troubleshooting convenience.

For inadvertent IMC, spatial disorientation, malfunction, or an IMC abort, maintain aircraft control, transition fully to instruments, and climb immediately toward the applicable ERAA or local safe-altitude guidance as conditions permit; squawk as required and tell ATC your intentions.
Do not rush into switches or a full emergency procedure while the aircraft is still not stabilized on instruments.
The pilot at the controls maintains aircraft control and executes critical action memory items and any actions directed by the PIC.
Use CRM early: verbalize the aircraft state, the altitude plan, the emergency, and what help you need from ATC or the other cockpit.
A good brief explains the first safe altitude, the transponder or radio call, and what would make the event a land-as-soon-as-practical or more urgent problem.

items.text: The GCA pattern packages radar-approach skills into one airwork profile: downwind, turns, BAC transition, controlled descent, heading corrections, missed approach, and level-off.

children.text: Start at 200 KIAS, clean, on a cardinal heading and base altitude to simulate radar downwind.
Turn standard rate, not to exceed 30 degrees AOB, for 90 degrees of heading change; maintain altitude and use the one-third rollout rule.
Slow toward 150 KIAS with about 15% torque, anticipate left rudder, trim through the deceleration, and stabilize near 33% torque at 150 KIAS.
Make the second same-direction 90-degree standard-rate turn, again preserving altitude and leading rollout with the one-third rule.
Maintain heading and altitude while transitioning to BAC: reduce power to about 15%, check below 150 KIAS, lower gear and set flaps to T/O.
Expect added lift with flaps; use slight nose-low pressure to hold altitude and trim right rudder plus up elevator as the aircraft slows.
Execute the Before Landing Checklist and stabilize at 120 KIAS with about 42% torque.
After stabilizing, set about 24% torque, let the nose fall enough to hold 120 KIAS, and establish roughly 600 FPM for a 2000-foot simulated GCA descent.
The instructor may give 3- to 10-degree heading changes during the descent; do not let the corrections disrupt airspeed or rate.
Remember the FTI control split: nose controls airspeed and power controls rate of descent, but each input affects the other.
After the 2000-foot descent, execute the missed approach: max power, right rudder, and 10 to 15 degrees nose high.
Check VSI and altimeter for positive climb, call two positive rates and raise the gear.
Above 110 KIAS, raise the flaps; report gear and flaps up before 150 KIAS, then set 8 to 10 degrees nose high and accelerate toward 180 KIAS.
Climb for 2000 feet on the last assigned heading, then start the 200 KIAS cruise transition about 200 feet before level-off.
The maneuver is complete at the original altitude, 200 KIAS, and the last assigned heading.
Common errors are poor power/nose coordination in the descent, over-rotating on the missed approach, late gear or flap cleanup, and weak rudder trim that lets heading drift.

items.text: The S-1 pattern is a timing and scan drill: hold 150 KIAS and heading while flying two 1000-foot descents and two 1000-foot climbs at about 1000 FPM.

children.text: Start clean at 150 KIAS on any numbered or cardinal heading.
Use timing checkpoints every 250 feet; at 1000 FPM each 250-foot altitude change should take about 15 seconds.
Lead the clock by 3 seconds before 00 or 30 seconds so the new power and attitude picture is established on time.
For the descent, reduce power to about 15%, lower the nose to about 0 degrees, anticipate left rudder, and re-trim.
Maintain 150 KIAS with nose attitude and adjust power as required for rate.
At each 250 feet, check the clock for 15 seconds elapsed and decide whether you are ahead or behind.
Three seconds before the end of one minute or 50 feet before the end of the 1000-foot descent, whichever occurs first, add power to about 55% and raise the nose to about 6 degrees nose high.
Anticipate right rudder, re-trim, then continue to hold 150 KIAS with pitch and use power to correct the climb rate.
At the next transition, repeat the descent and climb using the same 3-second lead and 50-foot level-off cue.
About 50 feet before the final altitude, transition to level flight at 150 KIAS on the original altitude regardless of rate.
The maneuver is complete when heading, altitude, airspeed, and trim are stable after the second climb.
Pitch primarily controls airspeed and power primarily controls vertical rate, but changing one will still affect the other.
Common errors are weak rudder trim, late or incorrect power settings, swapping pitch and power roles, and confusing ahead versus behind timing corrections.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: The approach maneuver simulates a low-altitude instrument approach from over a NAVAID while forcing clean scan, timing, descent control, BAC transition, and missed-approach discipline.

children.text: Start at 200 KIAS in straight-and-level flight on a cardinal heading.
Slow toward 150 KIAS with about 15% torque; anticipate left rudder and trim right rudder plus up elevator as the aircraft decelerates.
Approaching 150 KIAS, add power to about 33% to maintain level flight and re-trim.
Turn right standard rate, not to exceed 30 degrees AOB, for 90 degrees of heading change while maintaining altitude and using the one-third rollout rule.
After the 90-degree turn, start the clock for two minutes, set about 15% torque, and descend 1000 feet at 150 KIAS and about 1000 FPM.
About 100 feet before level-off, add power to about 33% and level at 150 KIAS.
At the end of two minutes, begin a left standard-rate turn for 210 degrees; anticipate a small need for power and back-stick pressure to hold level flight at 150 KIAS.
After the 210-degree turn, slow down first, then go down: reduce power to about 15% and maintain altitude to expedite deceleration.
Below 150 KIAS, lower the gear, set flaps to T/O, and execute the Before Landing Checklist.
At 120 KIAS, lower the nose and descend 1000 feet; about 100 feet before level-off, add power to about 42% to maintain 120 KIAS.
Stabilize on altitude and heading, reset the clock, set about 15% torque again, and descend another 1000 feet at 120 KIAS and about 1000 FPM.
At the end of the second two-minute timing segment, execute the missed approach: max power, right rudder, and 10 to 15 degrees nose high.
Check VSI and altimeter, call two positive rates and raise the gear; above 110 KIAS, raise the flaps.
Report gear and flaps up before 150 KIAS, then set 8 to 10 degrees nose high and accelerate toward 180 KIAS while climbing 2000 feet.
Start the 200 KIAS cruise transition about 200 feet before level-off.
The maneuver is complete at 200 KIAS, on the heading used after the 210-degree turn, and 1000 feet below the original starting altitude.

The event's special navigation requirement is to proceed direct to homefield using an available NAVAID when directed; brief the navigation method as part of the approach setup, not as a separate discussion item.
Common errors are late power changes, poor trim through BAC, chasing rate with pitch instead of power, and missing gear/flap cleanup during the missed approach.

items.text: IFR unusual-attitude recovery is an instrument scan and verification problem: recognize the bad attitude, confirm it against backup/performance instruments, and recover without creating a worse energy state.

children.text: An unusual attitude is any unexpected or inadvertent attitude encountered during normal instrument flight.
To avoid the situation in IMC, roll should normally be limited to 30 degrees AOB, nose low to 10 degrees, and nose high to 15 degrees.
Common causes include slow scan, spatial disorientation, fixation on a subtask, and transition from VFR to IFR.
Recognize with attitude indicator and performance cues, then confirm actual attitude with the BFI and performance instruments before recovering.
Relax back-stick pressure while maintaining positive G so the nose can fall toward the horizon.
Roll toward, but not past, 90 degrees of bank; use only as much bank as needed.
If climbing, use power as required to keep airspeed above stall.
As the miniature aircraft approaches the horizon, adjust bank toward wings level; if airspeed is below 100 KIAS, the nose may continue below the horizon until safe flying speed is restored.
Roll wings level first.
Start the pull only after the wings are level.
Approaching 200 KIAS or greater, reduce power and use speed brake if required to stay below maximum allowable airspeed.
Recovery is complete when the aircraft is back in the desired attitude for normal instrument flight.
Common nose-high errors are pushing negative G, not rolling enough toward 90 degrees when needed, and failing to add power.
Common nose-low errors are pulling before wings level and forgetting to reset power or speed brake after recovery.

items.text: In I2103, IMC emergency thinking is tied directly to unusual attitudes and avionics failures: stabilize first, then troubleshoot.

children.text: Use the NATOPS emergency priorities: maintain aircraft control, analyze the situation and take proper action, then land as soon as conditions permit.
Critical action memory items are completed immediately when required; time permitting, back them up with the checklist.
In IMC, protect altitude, attitude, terrain clearance, and ATC coordination before local convenience or troubleshooting flow.

For inadvertent IMC, spatial disorientation, malfunction, or an IMC abort, maintain aircraft control, transition fully to instruments, and climb immediately toward the applicable ERAA or local safe-altitude guidance as conditions permit.
Squawk and declare as required, tell ATC your intentions, and avoid a heads-down troubleshooting posture until the aircraft is stable.
If the emergency is an avionics failure, transition to the BFI or remaining reliable instruments before touching repeat switches or circuit breakers.

items.text: Dual IAC failure is an avionics-failure event that can remove the normal flight-display picture; the first answer is to fly the aircraft from backup references before troubleshooting.

children.text: Dual IAC failure results in loss of HUD, UFCP, and MFD displays in both cockpits.
A single IAC failure may not show an IAC failure message, but may cause MFD loss in one or both cockpits, erratic MFD behavior, HUD or UFCP malfunction, or synchronization errors.
Synchronization errors can show up as mismatched heading, altitude, or airspeed bugs between cockpits, QNH DISAGREE on the FMS, or incorrect REPEAT-mode behavior.
If synchronization errors or erratic indications are detected on the ground, takeoff is not recommended.
If synchronization errors exist without MFD loss, do not select REPEAT in either cockpit.
Do not select REPEAT from a cockpit with working MFDs during suspected crosstalk or synchronization failure; it may lead to loss of all MFD information in both cockpits.
Reference the BFI as required.
Set the NORM/REPEAT switch to NORM in both cockpits.
Check IAC1 and IAC2 circuit breakers on the left and right front console and reset if open.
If IAC/MFD failures or erratic displays persist, pull the failed IAC circuit breaker or breakers, then reset after 5 seconds.
If failures, erratic displays, or synchronization errors persist, land as soon as practical.

items.text: The BFI is the backup attitude and performance reference that keeps the aircraft flyable after PFD, ADC, IRU, or IAC failures.

children.text: The BFI is in the upper right side of the instrument panel in both cockpits.
It provides attitude, altitude, airspeed, heading, and vertical velocity.
It is normally powered by the battery bus; with a battery-bus failure, the auxiliary battery can power it through the AUX BAT switch.
The front cockpit circuit breaker is STBY INST; rear cockpit BFI power is through AFT STBY on the front-cockpit panel.
The adjustment knob changes baro; pushing it sets STD 29.92.
The M push-button enters or exits menu mode.
Useful menu items include FAST ERECT, SET BRIGHTNESS, FAST ALIGN, and SET HEADING when no external heading data is available.
FAST ERECT requires straight-and-level, non-accelerated flight.
If the PFD is partly or fully lost, reference the BFI, smoothly level the wings with coordinated rudder and aileron, and set the nose to straight-and-level attitude.
Once the aircraft is stabilized, complete the applicable NATOPS emergency procedure.
The common error is rushing into an emergency procedure before the aircraft is stabilized in straight-and-level BFI flight.
ATT FAIL removes pitch ladder, roll pointer, and slip/skid while leaving roll scale and aircraft symbol on a cyan background.
Processor errors may show as a red X or a black screen with instructions.

studyNotes.summary: Fly the approach maneuver precisely, then show that unusual attitudes, IMC emergencies, IAC failures, and BFI-only flight all start with the same control-first instrument discipline.

events.overview: I2201 turns the HSI into a usable position picture. The event standard is to know where the station, aircraft, bearing pointer, and CDI are telling you to go, then use that picture to go direct, track, identify station passage, and intercept radials without chasing the display.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: HSI orientation starts with a mental model: the NAVAID is at the center of the compass card, and the aircraft is on the tail of the bearing pointer.

children.text: The compass rose rotates with aircraft heading; the aircraft symbol stays fixed at the top of the display.
Bearing pointer #1 is the green single-line pointer and bearing pointer #2 is the cyan double-line pointer; the head points toward the selected source and the tail shows the radial you are on.

The CDI course arrow shows the selected VOR course or FMS track, the deviation bar shows lateral displacement, and the TO/FROM arrow tells whether that selected course is taking you to or from the station.
Unless you are tracking directly to or from the NAVAID, forward motion makes heads fall and tails rise.
Tie every answer back to present position: station in the center, aircraft on the tail, desired course in the CDI, and turn direction from the relationship between them.
The event may remove CDI help and require bearing-pointer/heading-bug work, so brief the bearing-pointer logic instead of memorizing one display setup.
Common errors are reading the head as aircraft position, forgetting the TO/FROM meaning, and treating bearing-pointer motion as a command instead of an orientation cue.

items.text: Going direct to a VOR is a setup-and-track procedure: tune the correct station, point at it, center a TO course, then keep the course centered with wind correction.

children.text: Tune, identify, and monitor the desired VOR before trusting the display.
Select PFD source to VOR and select bearing pointer #1 to VOR.
Turn the shortest direction to place the head of bearing pointer #1 under the heading index.
Set a CDI course that centers the CDI with a TO indication; the PFD press-and-hold function can do this quickly.
Track the new course by flying a heading that keeps the CDI centered.
Do not skip station identification or fly to the wrong source just because a pointer is displayed.
A centered CDI is not the finish line; the next task is tracking, because wind will move the aircraft off the direct course unless you correct.

items.text: Tracking is not homing. Homing keeps turning toward the station; tracking corrects for wind so the ground track stays on the selected course.

children.text: Once established on course, hold heading equal to course until CDI or bearing-pointer movement shows drift.
Use tail-radial-wind: draw from the bearing-pointer tail toward the desired radial to visualize where the wind is coming from.
Use tail-radial-turn or the CDI bar to decide the turn back toward course; the aircraft symbol is where you are, and the deviation bar is where you need to go.
Use an intercept angle suited to distance and closure; other than extreme cases, 45 degrees should be the maximum needed.
After re-intercepting, crab into the wind to hold the course. If unsure, start with about 5 degrees and watch whether the CDI drifts the same way, reverses, or stays centered.
Near the station, CDI and bearing-pointer sensitivity increase because radial spacing tightens; keep corrections within about 10 degrees of wind-corrected heading to avoid chasing needles.
The event specifically values bearing-pointer-only orientation, so be ready to explain the same correction without a CDI.

items.text: Station passage is primarily recognized by the first positive TO-to-FROM change on the CDI as the aircraft passes directly over or abeam the radio facility.

children.text: Expect bearing-pointer and CDI sensitivity to increase close to a conventional NAVAID; do not treat every jump in the cone of confusion as a heading command.
Hold the planned wind-corrected heading through the unreliable portion instead of chasing rapid pointer movement.
After passage, let the bearing pointer stabilize before building the outbound intercept picture.

items.text: An over-the-station intercept is used to intercept and fly outbound on a specified radial immediately after station passage.

children.text: Use the six Ts one at a time: time as required, turn, time as required, transition, twist/intercept, and talk.

Turn the shortest direction to parallel or intercept the outbound course. For small course changes, parallel while the bearing pointer stabilizes; for course changes greater than 90 degrees, turn to an intercept heading.
Do not turn more than 45 degrees beyond the heading needed to parallel the new course.
Set the new outbound course in the CDI, confirm FROM, then use double-the-angle up to 45 degrees once the bearing pointer is stable.
Maintain the intercept heading until able to make a standard-rate turn onto the new course, then make required voice reports.
The goal is not to spin knobs perfectly while task-saturated; it is to keep the airplane controlled, start the correct outbound geometry, and establish the new course without delay.
Common errors are too much intercept, too little intercept, delaying the intercept setup, and trying to solve the whole six-T sequence at once.

items.text: Radial intercept procedures position the aircraft on a nearby radial or course without passing over the station.

children.text: Tune, identify, and monitor the NAVAID.
Set the new course in the CDI: outbound uses the radial itself, while inbound uses the reciprocal.
Turn toward the CDI deviation bar so the head of the course arrow ends up in the top half of the HSI, and use tail-radial-turn to verify turn direction.
Use an intercept angle greater than the number of radials off course, but do not exceed 90 degrees.
A 45-degree intercept is normally sufficient for inbound and outbound intercepts.
If you are within about 10 radials and the CDI or bearing pointer is rapidly moving toward course, use double-the-angle instead of forcing the full 45-degree intercept.
For outbound double-the-angle, count from the bearing-pointer tail to the new course; for inbound, count from the bearing-pointer head to the new course.
Maintain the intercept heading until you can make a standard-rate turn onto the course, then track the radial or course with wind correction.
Close to the station, pointer movement accelerates; plan the intercept early enough that sensitivity does not make you chase.
Common errors are setting the reciprocal wrong, turning away from the needed intercept, using the wrong pointer end, and joining with too much or too little intercept.

studyNotes.summary: Build the HSI picture first, then use bearing-pointer and CDI movement to go direct, track, identify station passage, and intercept radials without chasing needles.

events.overview: I2202 builds the geometry that makes radio navigation usable when the clearance is not simply direct-to or radial tracking. Be ready to compute arc lead points, leave an arc on time, solve point-to-point headings, and handle oxygen-system or physiological problems without losing the instrument scan.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Arcing is flying at a constant DME from a NAVAID. You approximate the arc with small heading and bank changes; you are not trying to draw a perfect circle.

children.text: Proceed direct to the arc entry point defined by radial and DME.
Calculate the lead point, determine the turn direction, and begin a standard-rate turn at the lead point.
Continue the turn until the bearing-pointer head is on the 90-degree benchmark for the arc direction.
Check DME immediately after rollout and correct early instead of waiting for a large displacement.
In no wind, bearing-pointer head on the 90-degree benchmark means DME is constant.
Bearing-pointer head below the 90-degree benchmark means DME is increasing.
Bearing-pointer head above the 90-degree benchmark means DME is decreasing.
If inside the arc, maintain heading or place the bearing-pointer head up to 15 degrees below the benchmark; if outside, place it up to 15 degrees above the benchmark.
Common errors are late lead-point planning, turning the wrong direction, and overcorrecting DME instead of making small benchmark changes.

items.text: A radial-arc intercept transitions from tracking a radial to joining an arc at a specified DME.

children.text: For a standard-rate 90-degree turn, turn radius is 0.5% of groundspeed in NM; for example, 150 knots is about 0.75 NM.
If groundspeed is not available in time, KIAS may be used as a no-wind approximation.
When a full standard-rate turn is not appropriate, use 1.0% of groundspeed for a half-standard-rate lead point.
Apply the turn radius so the aircraft begins turning before the arc DME, then adjust for known wind.
Start the turn at the computed DME and roll toward the 90-degree bearing-pointer benchmark.
Check whether the first DME trend puts you inside or outside the arc, then correct with the arcing benchmark logic.
The briefing-guide emphasis is to know turn direction from the assigned arc direction before reaching the lead point.

items.text: An arc-radial intercept leaves an arc and joins an inbound or outbound radial. The key is calculating the lead radial early enough that the turn finishes on course.

children.text: Find radials per NM with the 60-to-1 rule: 60 divided by arc DME.
Find turn radius: 0.5% of groundspeed for standard-rate, or 1.0% for half-standard-rate.
Multiply turn radius by radials per NM; that product is the no-wind lead radial.
Set the CDI for the course you will intercept before reaching the lead radial, then begin the turn at the lead radial.
Greater arc DME means fewer lead radials because radials are farther apart.
Half-standard-rate turns need more lead radials than standard-rate turns because the turn takes longer.
Adjust the no-wind lead for known wind, then track the new radial or course after rollout.

items.text: An OBOGS malfunction is a crew-survival problem before it is a system-analysis problem. Keep flying, get a secure oxygen source, descend when required, and use the checklist.

children.text: An OBOGS FAIL warning can indicate low bleed-air pressure, low oxygen concentration, or an internal failure detected by the system.
OBOGS TEMP indicates a heat-exchanger failure and is treated as an OBOGS failure.
Physiological symptoms or zeolite-dust indications can occur without a warning light; coughing, respiratory irritation, or white dust in the mask still demand immediate action.
Engine failure, total electrical failure, main battery depletion, or battery failure removes OBOGS support.
Check both cockpits: supply ON, concentration MAX, pressure EMERGENCY, flow indication, hose/CRU-60/P connection, and mask seal.
If symptoms are recognized, immediately execute the OBOGS Failure/Overtemp/Physiological Symptoms procedure instead of troubleshooting first.
Emergency oxygen provides about 10 minutes; above 10,000 feet cockpit altitude, pulling the green ring is required before depletion risk becomes incapacitating.
Initiate descent below 10,000 feet MSL, secure OBOGS supply OFF as directed, and land as soon as practical.

items.text: Hypoxia and hyperventilation can feel similar early, so the safe cockpit answer is to protect oxygen first, then normalize breathing once the oxygen source is secure.

children.text: Hypoxia is oxygen deficiency in body tissues; early signs can include poor judgment, euphoria, fatigue, tunnel vision, dizziness, or headache.
Advanced hypoxia can progress to cyanosis, confusion, loss of coordination, unconsciousness, and incapacitation.
Susceptibility increases with factors such as fatigue, dehydration, illness, alcohol, medication, smoking, carbon monoxide exposure, temperature stress, and exertion.
Hyperventilation is abnormally rapid or deep breathing that lowers carbon dioxide.
Symptoms can include lightheadedness, tingling, drowsiness, muscle spasms, a feeling of suffocation, and in severe cases unconsciousness.
When breathing oxygen under increased pressure, breathe slightly slower and shallower than normal to avoid inducing hyperventilation.
If unsure which one you have, treat it like hypoxia first: secure oxygen, verify flow, descend as required, tell the other cockpit, then consciously slow and normalize breathing.
Do not let symptom analysis pull both pilots heads-down; keep one pilot flying and scanning.

items.text: Point-to-point navigation uses a VOR/DME or VORTAC to fly directly from present position to a radial/DME fix without waiting for radar vectors.

children.text: Tune, identify, and monitor the NAVAID.
Set the desired radial in the CDI; this helps build the picture even when it is not the heading you will fly.
Visualize the station at the center of the HSI compass card.
Plot the fix with the greater DME on the edge of the compass card and the smaller-DME fix proportionally closer to center.
Turn initially to a heading between the bearing-pointer head and the course-pointer head: split the heads.
Favor the bearing-pointer head when going to a smaller DME; favor the course-pointer head when going to a larger DME.
Use the pencil method to draw the present-position-to-desired-fix line, move that line to the center of the card, and read the updated no-wind heading.
Keep updating en route. If the line tilts right, turn right; if it tilts left, turn left.
As you near the fix, compare DME rate to radial-crossing rate.
If arriving at DME first, use the 90-degree benchmark to split the bearing pointer and desired radial; do not arc to the radial.
If arriving at the radial first, turn to track inbound or outbound as required toward the fix.
Common errors are delaying the initial turn, splitting the wrong heads, using the reciprocal radial, failing to update the pencil solution, and trying to arc to the fix.

studyNotes.summary: Lead the arc, manage DME with bearing-pointer benchmarks, solve point-to-point geometry early, and treat oxygen or physiological symptoms as immediate crew-survival problems.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Holding entry begins before the fix: copy the clearance, determine the holding side and pattern direction, slow in time, and know the first outbound heading before crossing.

children.text: Start the speed reduction within 3 minutes or 5 NM of the holding fix when clearance beyond the fix has not been received.
The normal T-6B holding airspeed is 150 KIAS; published maximum holding speeds still matter for altitude and field-specific restrictions.
A standard pattern uses right turns; a non-standard pattern uses left turns. If turn direction is not stated, right turns are implied.
If timing is used, the inbound leg is normally 1 minute at or below 14,000 feet MSL and 1 1/2 minutes above 14,000 feet MSL.

For a standard pattern, parallel entry is used when the reciprocal of the holding course lies between the heading index and 110 degrees left; teardrop is between the heading index and 70 degrees right; otherwise use direct entry.
For a non-standard pattern, mirror the logic: parallel is to the right, teardrop is to the left, and direct is the remaining sector.
Standard teardrop heading is 30 degrees less than the reciprocal of the holding course; non-standard teardrop heading is 30 degrees more.
If the reciprocal is within 5 degrees of an entry boundary, either entry is acceptable.
Use the six Ts to keep task order clean: time, turn, time, transition, twist, talk.
Report established in holding with position, time, and altitude when required; confirm EFC at least 5 minutes prior if needed.
At the end of the outbound leg, turn inbound toward the holding radial using tail-radial-turn and intercept the holding course promptly.

items.text: The no-wind orbit begins on the second passage of the holding fix and gives you the information needed to correct both heading and timing.

children.text: Cross the fix, reset elapsed time, and turn in the pattern direction to the no-wind outbound heading, which is the reciprocal of the holding course.
Start outbound timing when wings level or abeam the holding fix, whichever occurs last.
If abeam cannot be determined, start timing when wings level.
At the end of the outbound leg, turn inbound toward the holding radial and start inbound timing when wings level on course or with an appropriate intercept established.
An on-course inbound rollout suggests no crosswind component.
An undershoot suggests crosswind from the non-holding side.
An overshoot suggests crosswind from the holding side.
Once established inbound, use normal tracking procedures to find the wind-corrected heading and note the crab angle.
Note inbound time at the fix if timing corrections are required for the next orbit.
Keep basic airwork clean; altitude, heading, and airspeed errors contaminate the wind picture you are trying to measure.

items.text: Holding corrections apply the no-wind orbit lesson: correct outbound heading for drift, adjust outbound time for inbound timing, then refine on each orbit.

children.text: Triple the inbound drift correction for the outbound leg; for example, an 8-degree right crab inbound becomes a 24-degree left correction outbound.
Hold triple drift for no more than 1 minute outbound.
If the outbound leg continues beyond 1 minute, transition to single drift for the remaining time.
If no-wind inbound time exceeded 90 seconds, the first wind-corrected outbound time should be no less than 30 seconds.
Adjust outbound time to fix the previous inbound time. If inbound was 10 seconds short, add 10 seconds outbound; if inbound was long, subtract time.
Subsequent orbits are fine-tuning passes, not proof that the first correction was bad.
Inbound legs are tracked on the holding course; outbound legs are flown as headings.
Keep fuel and EFC time in the scan, especially in stacked holding where vertical separation can be as little as 1000 feet.

Common errors are using the drift correction in the wrong direction, forgetting to transition from triple drift to single drift, trying to track outbound, and letting basic airwork or magnetic-variation confusion drive false corrections.

items.text: Battery and generator failure assumes the generator has failed and the main battery is depleted. In IMC, the problem is maintaining control with a stripped cockpit while getting below oxygen and pressurization risk.

children.text: Only auxiliary-battery-powered essentials remain: backup flight instrument, FIRE 1 detection, IRU, and VHF radio through the standby VHF control head.

Major losses include OBOGS, ICS, all electronic displays, PMU, starter, FIRE 2, landing-gear indicators, normal flap operation and indications, probes anti-ice, interior/exterior lighting, ECS/pressurization, UHF, GPS, VHF NAV, DME, transponder, and TCAS.
OBOGS is inoperative once the main battery is depleted or with battery failure, and the cockpit will depressurize when power to the battery bus is lost.
Initiate descent below 10,000 feet MSL as required.
Turn AUX BAT ON to power the backup flight instrument and standby VHF path for about 30 minutes.
Plan to extend the landing gear with the emergency extension system; emergency flaps will not be available if the main battery has failed, and flaps may retract if battery-bus power is lost.
Land as soon as possible.
In an instrument event, immediately transition your scan to the BFI, preserve attitude and airspeed, and use standby VHF/ATC help before task-saturating on lost displays.
A PAR or ASR/no-gyro recovery may be feasible if conditions, communication, and remaining instruments support it; brief it as a recovery option, not a guarantee.

studyNotes.summary: Enter holding deliberately, use the no-wind orbit to measure wind, correct with triple drift and timing, and keep the BFI/standby-VHF recovery plan ready for battery and generator failure.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Clearance and departure procedures connect the IFR clearance, the departure method, and the instrument takeoff scan into one plan before the aircraft moves.

children.text: Copy the clearance deliberately: aircraft identification, clearance limit, departure type, route, altitude, departure frequency, transponder code, and any additional restrictions or holding instructions.
Before takeoff, review terrain, hazards, climb gradients, and the assigned departure type; set NAVAIDs and displays so the first navigation task is ready before brake release.
Keep the most likely emergency return approach available. Departure setup should answer where you will point the aircraft if the climb does not go normally.
Fly a normal takeoff, use outside references and the attitude indicator at liftoff, then transition fully to the instrument scan as visual cues diminish.
Set about 8 to 10 degrees nose high, trim, verify the climb on the altimeter and VSI, then raise the gear and flaps.
Maintain the initial attitude until about 180 KIAS unless the departure or aircraft performance requires a different climb profile.
For best-rate climb, use about 140 KIAS and 15 degrees nose high.
Lead level-offs with roughly 10 percent of the climb rate; for example, start adjusting about 200 feet early during a 2000 FPM climb.
If below climb speed, reduce power as the pitch comes down. If above climb speed, maintain power long enough to accelerate, then stabilize and trim.
Know the departure families: ODP, SID, radar departure, diverse departure, and VCOA.
For a diverse departure, climb to 400 feet AGL before turning and plan on at least 200 feet per NM, which is about 600 FPM at 180 KIAS.

items.text: En route procedures are the discipline that keeps the aircraft ahead of the next clearance, fix, approach setup, and descent requirement.

children.text: Use the assigned airway, radial, DME, or point-to-point clearance as the controlling navigation task; FMS shortcuts do not replace the radio-navigation procedure being trained.

For point-to-point navigation, tune and identify the NAVAID, set the desired radial, visualize the present and desired radial/DME positions, then split the bearing-pointer and course-pointer heads for the initial no-wind heading.
Update the point-to-point solution as DME and bearing change. If DME will arrive first, split the needle to slow DME change; if the radial arrives first, track inbound or outbound to the fix.
Use the ABCDs early enough to matter: ATIS, brief the approach and minimums, cockpit setup, and descent checklist before the IAF.
Plan NAVAID changeover at the published changeover point, halfway between facilities if no point is shown, or about 10 NM before an intersection when required.
Keep fuel, weather, recovery options, and approach request timing in the scan instead of waiting for the terminal area to force the workload.

items.text: A procedure turn reverses course inside protected airspace so the aircraft can intercept the final approach course from the proper side and altitude.

children.text: Do not fly a procedure turn when SNERT applies: straight-in clearance, NoPT routing, established in aligned holding and cleared for the approach, radar vectors to final, or a timed approach.
About 5 NM before the IAF, slow to 150 KIAS and prepare the six Ts.
At station passage, turn the shortest direction to parallel the outbound course. If that turn would exceed 90 degrees, use a 45-degree intercept.
Start 1 minute outbound when wings level or abeam, whichever occurs later; descend if required with about 15 percent torque at 150 KIAS.
Level at the procedure-turn altitude, normally adding power near 33 percent torque and re-trimming.
At 1 minute outbound, turn 45 degrees toward the protected side, start another 1-minute clock, and twist the inbound course.

At the end of the barb leg, turn 180 degrees opposite. If the bearing-pointer head is within 5 degrees of the inbound course, continue the turn with double-the-angle intercept; otherwise roll out on the barb heading for a 45-degree intercept.
Within 5 NM of the FAF, transition to before-approach configuration and maintain altitude until slowing permits the descent.

items.text: A teardrop approach is another course-reversal option that uses an offset outbound leg toward the protected side before turning inbound.

children.text: A non-depicted teardrop may be used as a substitute for a depicted procedure turn when cleared for the approach; offset about 20 degrees from the final approach course toward the barb or protected side.
Remain within the published distance, typically 10 NM, and adjust the outbound leg for wind so the turn back inbound stays inside protected airspace.
About 5 NM before the IAF, slow to 150 KIAS.
At station passage, turn toward the outbound teardrop course, start 2 minutes outbound when wings level or abeam, and descend if required with about 15 percent torque at 150 KIAS.
Level at the procedure-turn altitude, add power near 33 percent torque, and twist the inbound course at about 1.5 minutes outbound.
At 2 minutes outbound, turn in the depicted direction. Use double-the-angle if the bearing-pointer head is within 5 degrees of inbound; otherwise use a 45-degree intercept.
Transition to before-approach configuration within 5 NM of the FAF and continue with the published approach.

items.text: Arcing approaches use DME to move around a facility until a lead radial or turn point places the aircraft on the final approach course.

children.text: Confirm DME is required by the approach title or equipment notes, such as VOR/DME or TACAN.
At the IAF, turn to place the bearing pointer on the 90-degree benchmark, comply with segment altitudes, and set the inbound course in the CDI.
Use radial-to-arc and arc-to-radial intercept techniques rather than chasing the needle after the turn point has passed.
For radial-to-arc intercepts, standard-rate lead DME is about 0.5 percent of groundspeed; half-standard-rate lead DME is about 1 percent of groundspeed.
For arc-to-radial intercepts, estimate radials per NM as 60 divided by arc DME, then multiply by turn radius to find the lead radial.
Published lead radials are normally based on 200 KTAS and half-standard-rate turns; at 150 KIAS, compute a standard-rate lead and adjust for wind.
Within 5 NM of the FAF, transition to before-approach configuration and continue inbound on the published approach.

items.text: Missed approach procedures protect the climb after an approach can no longer be continued visually, safely, or within course guidance.

children.text: Execute the missed approach at the MAP or DA/DH when the runway environment is not in sight, required visibility is not available, or the aircraft is not in position for a normal landing.
If full-scale CDI deflection occurs before the FAF, attempt to re-intercept, do not descend, and notify ATC.
If full-scale CDI deflection occurs between the FAF and MAP, climb toward the missed-approach altitude and notify ATC. Obstacle protection is only assured along published or assigned segments.
In training, distinguish the published missed approach from an assigned climbout; fly the clearance you were given unless safety requires otherwise.
At the MAP, set PCL MAX, pitch 10 to 15 degrees nose high, verify two positive rates, then raise the gear.
Above 110 KIAS, raise the flaps, accelerate toward 180 KIAS, and adjust toward an 8 to 10 degree nose-high climb attitude.
Start a standard-rate turn as required to the missed-approach course or assigned heading, then report missed approach with the reason.
Once climbing and navigating, pass DRAFT as required: destination, route, altitude, fuel, and time en route.
Standard obstacle-clearance planning uses 200 feet per NM; the T-6B normally exceeds that at about 180 KIAS and roughly 2000 FPM, but higher published gradients still require performance planning.

studyNotes.summary: Copy and fly the IFR clearance, transition from takeoff to instruments, manage en route setup, and execute PT, teardrop, arcing, and missed-approach procedures with disciplined task flow.
