events.overview: F4101 brings formation fundamentals into the aircraft. The brief should cover signal discipline, lead and wing responsibilities, abort contracts, lost-sight and blind procedures, and the HEFOE system so the section can preserve separation when normal visual or radio communication breaks down.

notes: Adjust specifics to match the assigned profile, weather, and local procedures.
Because the blocks are shared, one edit updates every event that references the same procedure or comm call.
scriptTemplate.title: F4101 Script

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Hand signals are formation commands. They must be passed where Wing can see them, acknowledged clearly, and backed up by radio when the situation is unclear.

children.text: Lead confirms Wing is in position, clears the area, passes the signal high and visible, then looks back for Wing's acknowledgment.
Wing acknowledges with a deliberate head nod or gives a no-head-shake if the signal is missed or unclear.
Lead executes only after acknowledgment unless the signal itself is an immediate safety-of-flight command.
Use radio calls in IMC, when a visual signal could be missed, or anytime confusion exists.
Do not force a visual-signal answer if aircraft control, spacing, or weather makes a radio call safer.

items.text: Lead and Wing share the sortie, but they do not share the same immediate job.

children.text: The Designated Flight Lead is administratively responsible for mission objectives and safe, orderly conduct.
The Formation Lead is the aircraft physically flying lead at the moment.
Lead must be smooth, stable, predictable, and directive.
Lead must keep the flight clear of clouds unless on an IFR clearance, clear of other aircraft, and within the assigned area or route.
Keep Lead in sight and maintain deconfliction.
Maintain proper position and correct early with small inputs.
Comply with Lead's signals and respond promptly.
Back up navigation, communications, fuel awareness, and safety decisions.

items.text: An aborted takeoff in formation is a separation problem as much as an aircraft problem. Decide, stay on your side, and communicate as soon as aircraft control permits.

children.text: Brief abort contingencies before takeoff.
If aborting, execute the NATOPS abort procedure, maintain directional control, remain on the assigned runway side, and transmit intentions.
If Lead aborts during an interval takeoff, Wing normally aborts behind Lead while maintaining Wing's side; the 5-second interval should provide spacing.
If Wing aborts during an interval takeoff, Wing aborts on Wing's side and transmits once Lead is airborne and Wing is under control.
If either aircraft aborts after brake release, the aborting aircraft stays on its side and executes the abort.

The non-aborting aircraft recognizes the rapid line-of-sight change, selects maximum power, maintains side-of-runway discipline, and executes an individual takeoff unless separation cannot be maintained or it has its own emergency.
Wing must be prepared to avoid Lead if Lead loses directional control, including changing sides or leaving the prepared surface if required to prevent collision.
Aviate: control the aircraft.
Navigate: preserve runway-side separation and avoid the other aircraft.
Communicate: state intentions to the flight and tower when able.

items.text: Lost sight is an IMC procedure. Wing immediately transitions from formation references to instruments and creates predictable separation.

children.text: Transition to instrument scan and maintain aircraft control.
Call "lost sight" on the tactical frequency.
Smoothly reduce power about 10% to reduce closure risk.
Straight and level: Wing turns away for a 30-degree heading change, times for 30 seconds, then parallels Lead's heading.

Turns: the outside aircraft rolls wings level and transmits heading and altitude; the inside aircraft continues the turn for at least 30 degrees, then the outside aircraft turns to the assigned heading after 30 seconds.
Climbs or descents: Wing levels off, states altitude, and executes the applicable straight or turning lost-sight procedure while Lead continues to assigned altitude with at least 500 ft separation.
Inside the FAF, Wing turns away expeditiously, transitions to instruments, and calls lost sight.
Lead informs ATC and continues the approach.
Wing climbs to FAF or glideslope intercept altitude, proceeds to the MAP, and flies the missed approach unless ATC issues a new clearance.

items.text: Blind procedures are VMC procedures. The visual aircraft has deconfliction responsibility while the blind aircraft reports altitude and keeps looking.

children.text: Wing calls "blind" with altitude.
If Lead is visual, Lead directs Wing's eyes using clock position and high, level, or low references.
Wing continues to call "blind" or "visual" until Lead is reacquired.
If Wing calls visual, Lead directs the rejoin or continuation of training.
Lead transmits altitude, maneuvers predictably, and ensures at least 500 ft altitude separation without crossing altitudes.
Lead directs a rejoin at the briefed or alternate location.
Wing lags Lead's last known position, clears the flight path, follows directive instructions, and maintains altitude separation until visual.
TCAS may assist SA but is not the primary rejoin method.
If Wing is blind due to sun, Wing calls "blind sun" and lags Lead's last known position.
Lead calls continue only if deconfliction can be maintained; otherwise Lead calls knock-it-off.

items.text: HEFOE lets a NORDO aircraft communicate the affected system using visual signals.

children.text: Gain the other aircraft's attention first; the formation source uses a weeping signal before passing the affected system.
Use hand signals during day and flashlight signals at night if required.
The good-radio aircraft coordinates with ATC or tower and keeps the NORDO aircraft supported.
H: Hydraulics.
E: Electrical.
F: Fuel.
O: Oxygen.
E: Engine.

events.overview: F4102 shifts attention from basic position keeping to section problem solving. Students should brief how the section separates and supports an airborne damaged aircraft, how speed brake use is coordinated, how Lead manages area and sun exposure, and how lost communications are handled without losing formation discipline.

notes: Adjust specifics to match the assigned profile, weather, and local procedures.
Because the blocks are shared, one edit updates every event that references the same procedure or comm call.
scriptTemplate.title: F4102 Script

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Airborne damage is first an aircraft-control and deconfliction problem. The section does not rejoin just because both aircraft remain flyable.

children.text: Follow NATOPS procedures for the actual malfunction or damage.
If severe damage causes or may cause OCF, do not delay ejection beyond the safe envelope.
If damage is minimal, communicate, separate, maintain visual contact, and establish a deconfliction plan.
Use lateral, altitude, ground-reference, DME, or working-block separation as appropriate.
Do not rejoin the damaged aircraft as a flight.
Complete appropriate emergency checklists.
Consider assigning a chase or inspection aircraft if it can be done without adding risk.
Develop a recovery plan for both aircraft; if runway damage or FOD risk exists, consider separate airfields.
The damaged aircraft communicates if able, climbs to a safe altitude, and assumes Lead as necessary to assess the damage.
If forward visibility is lost or aircraft control is doubtful, controlled ejection may be required.
The good aircraft moves to perch and assists as required.

items.text: Speed brake use as a section must be predictable because extension, retraction, pitch change, and closure all affect Wing at once.

children.text: Lead may use speed brake to increase descent rate or decelerate the formation.
During recovery descents, Lead should normally use at least 15% torque.
Wing may need idle power and speed brake to maintain position.
Speed brake effectiveness decreases at lower airspeeds, and extension or retraction creates pitch changes that must be countered.
If Wing is in parade, Lead may direct speed brake with the visual signal and a head-nod acknowledgment.
If Wing is in cruise, Lead should use clear radio calls such as standby speed brake and speed brake now.
Lead must remain stable and avoid ambiguous timing.
In cruise, Wing may combine power, pursuit curves, and speed brake to move between parade and cruise or hold position.
During the fan break, Wing may use idle power and speed brake at maneuver start to create spacing.
If Lead is turning and Wing has excessive closure, Wing may need idle power and speed brake to avoid passing ahead.

sections.title: Speed Brake Use As a Section

items.text: Area and sun management are Lead responsibilities, but Wing should understand the plan so corrections and calls make sense.

children.text: Lead must know the assigned area boundaries and visualize how maneuver combinations will keep the flight inside them.
Wind affects ground track; Lead should plan turn direction and rollout timing before the edge of the area becomes urgent.
Formation tasks take longer than single-ship tasks, including radio changes, maneuvers, rejoins, and checklist work.
Lead should avoid prolonged straight-and-level or turn-into setups that force Wing to look into the sun.
Plan rollouts, crossunders, and maneuver sequencing to reduce Wing's sun exposure when practical.
Wing should call blind sun if Lead is temporarily lost in sun glare and then lag Lead's last known position.
Lead must be predictable and give Wing enough time to stabilize before the next maneuver.
If area, sun, or Wing position makes the next maneuver unsafe, use terminate or knock-it-off early.

items.text: Lost communication procedures keep the section VMC, deconflicted, and predictable while the affected aircraft troubleshoots.

children.text: Maintain VMC if able.
Gain the other aircraft's attention with visual signals.
If Wing is NORDO, Wing moves acute with lateral separation and passes the appropriate down-transmitter or down-receiver signal.
Offer the lead position to the NORDO aircraft so troubleshooting can be completed with less formation workload.
Check helmet and seat connections.
Verify frequency or channel selection.
Check audio-panel volume and radio selections.
Try available UHF, VHF, backup, and guard options as appropriate.
If radios cannot be restored, the good-radio aircraft should take or keep Lead for recovery coordination.
The good-radio aircraft informs ATC or tower of the NORDO aircraft and coordinates visual landing signals as required.
If an emergency occurs while NORDO, use HEFOE signals after gaining attention.
Use current local SOP and day-of brief for field-specific NORDO recovery details.

items.text: Speed Brake Use As a Section

events.overview: F4103 emphasizes the emergency side of formation: how to pass lead to the emergency aircraft, how Wing supports from perch, how section takeoff is flown and aborted, how emergency fields are selected, and how the section exits inadvertent instrument conditions without sacrificing separation.

notes: Adjust specifics to match the assigned profile, weather, and local procedures.
Because the blocks are shared, one edit updates every event that references the same procedure or comm call.
scriptTemplate.title: F4103 Script

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: A Section PEL starts by giving the emergency aircraft the maneuvering room and authority it needs while preserving mutual support.

children.text: If Lead has the emergency, Lead should make a quick radio call so Wing can get separation.
If Wing has the emergency, Wing requests lead left or right.
Lead transfers lead verbally only after visual contact and separation make the transfer safe.
The new Wing transitions to perch.
New Wing clears the flight path, provides divert or field information, assists with procedures if requested, and monitors altitude, airspeed, VSI, and configuration.
Wing matches the emergency aircraft's configuration when remaining through the profile.
The emergency aircraft maneuvers and configures for high key.
Lead may kiss off Wing at any time.
If Wing remains through the ELP, Wing stays outside Lead's turn and waves off when directed, no lower than 300 ft AGL.
Normally, Wing can safely detach and monitor at high key.

items.text: A section takeoff keeps both aircraft in formation from brake release through liftoff, so the brief must cover runway criteria, power timing, rotation, and abort responsibilities.

children.text: Runway must be at least 150 ft wide.
Maximum crosswind is 10 knots dry or 5 knots wet.
Weather must meet circling minimums, or 1000 ft ceiling and 3 SM visibility if circling minimums are not available.
Do not conduct a section takeoff with standing water on the runway.
Lead lines up on the downwind side unless calm winds or other briefed factors drive a different side.
Lead passes the run-up signal; both aircraft set about 30% torque.
Wing inspects Lead and holds thumbs-up until Lead acknowledges.
Lead's arm chop sets the power-advance rate; when the arm reaches the canopy rail, both aircraft release brakes.
Lead smoothly sets about 90% torque over roughly 5 seconds.
Wing maintains takeoff bearing with PCL and rudder; avoid riding the brakes, though one light tap may be used immediately after brake release if acute.
Lead rotates smoothly about 5 to 10 knots below normal rotation speed; local formation study material commonly uses 85 KIAS as the basic reference.
Wing matches Lead's attitude, remains briefly stepped up after liftoff, then waits for Lead's climb to establish safe step-down.
Lead signals or calls gear and flaps retraction at or above 110 KIAS; Wing retracts only after Lead.
If either aircraft aborts after brake release, maintain lateral control and do not cross the runway centerline.
The non-aborting aircraft normally selects maximum power and continues as an individual takeoff unless safe separation cannot be maintained or it has its own emergency.
Wing should always remain dirtier than Lead during cleanup; retract only after Lead is in transit.

items.text: Emergency field selection is a suitability and energy problem: choose a field the aircraft can reach and land on, then keep updating the plan as energy changes.

children.text: Prefer the closest suitable hard-surface runway at least 3000 ft long.
If multiple fields are available, consider crash crew, medical support, runway surface, wind, obstacles, and recovery complexity.
Use charts, NAVAIDs, FMS NAV/TSD, and nearest-airport tools to judge distance.
Use the DME method to judge one field: one-half DME plus key altitude plus field elevation equals the approximate MSL altitude required.
Add 3000 ft for high key or 1500 ft for low key when deciding if current energy is sufficient.
Use the altitude method to compare several fields: subtract 3000 ft for high key or 1500 ft for low key from AGL altitude, then multiply by 2 for maximum glide distance in NM.
Best-glide planning from the Contact FTI is about 125 KIAS clean, with roughly 2 NM per 1000 ft of altitude in no-wind conditions.
A zoom from high energy can increase altitude; local source material cites about 1300 ft gained from 240 KGS.
If no suitable landing area exists, NATOPS and Contact FTI guidance favor ejection when possible rather than pressing an unsuitable off-field landing.
If ejection is not possible or malfunctions, an ELP to an unprepared surface or ditching may be the remaining option, with higher injury and egress risk.

items.text: Inadvertent instrument flight in formation requires Lead to fly instruments while Wing maintains parade and prepares for lost-sight execution if visual references fail.

children.text: Lead transitions to an instrument scan and determines the safest way to exit IMC.
Wing maintains parade position and scans Lead.
If unable to regain VMC, Lead ensures terrain clearance and coordinates an IFR clearance for the flight or individual clearances at Flight Lead discretion.
If Wing loses sight of Lead, Wing immediately executes lost sight procedures.
Lead must stay directive and predictable so ATC coordination and separation do not conflict.

studyNotes.summary: F4103 is a formation emergency-management event: transfer lead when needed, support from perch, preserve runway-side discipline, select emergency fields, and keep the section separated in IMC.

events.overview: F4104 combines formation emergency support with dynamic maneuvering. Students should be able to brief an airborne landing gear inspection, distinguish knock-it-off from terminate, execute cruise maneuvering with pursuit geometry, and explain the lead principles that keep Wing predictable and safe.

notes: Adjust specifics to match the assigned profile, weather, and local procedures.
Because the blocks are shared, one edit updates every event that references the same procedure or comm call.
scriptTemplate.title: F4104 Script

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: A landing gear inspection is an emergency-support task, not a formation proficiency stunt. The inspection is flown only when it can be done without adding risk.

children.text: The aircraft with the unsafe indication notifies the other aircraft and ATC.
Climb to the published emergency orbit, delta pattern, or other local procedure before troubleshooting.
Request an airborne gear inspection if it will help the decision and can be done safely.
Wing follows the distressed aircraft and assists as directed.
Conduct the inspection at a minimum of 2000 ft AGL.
Use a discrete frequency when practical to reduce chatter and confusion.
The emergency aircraft communicates configuration, airspeed, altitude, and planned changes.
The inspecting aircraft reports position and intentions and avoids undue risk.
Use caution if visible damage could allow gear parts to depart the aircraft.
Student solos shall not join up to inspect landing gear.
Students shall not be at the controls during the landing gear inspection.
The emergency aircraft may ask Wing, chase, base, or RDO to help read checklists and troubleshoot.

items.text: Knock-it-off stops the maneuvering because safety is compromised or could be compromised.

children.text: Any flight member may initiate knock-it-off.
Use it for emergencies, traffic conflicts, blind situations, G-LOC or AGSM failure, area boundary concerns, or any developing unsafe condition.
The pilot calling knock-it-off should state the reason if able.
Lead maneuvers predictably, normally straight-and-level or with shallow bank.
Lead gives directive intentions and may state altitude and a reference heading for the flight.
Both aircraft prioritize separation and aircraft control before resuming any training objective.

items.text: Terminate stops an exercise or maneuvering for an expected or administrative reason; it is not the same as knock-it-off.

children.text: Lead normally initiates terminate, but Wing may request or initiate it.
Use terminate when the training objective is complete, the exercise is ending, or continuing would not be useful.
If the reason is safety-of-flight, call knock-it-off instead.
Lead remains predictable and transitions to a safe attitude.
Lead directs follow-on intentions, such as cleared to parade, continue, repeat, or recover.
Wing maintains deconfliction and does not rush the rejoin.

items.text: Cruise maneuvering teaches Wing to maintain position with pursuit geometry and lift-vector placement, not constant power chasing.

children.text: Lead signals cruise and holds a stable platform until Wing is established.
Wing acknowledges, slides to the 60-degree bearing line, sets the directed power, and calls ready.
Formation FTI references use about 80% torque above 10,000 ft and 70% torque below 10,000 ft before maneuvering; hold the PCL position rather than chasing torque changes with altitude.
Cruise position is about 60 degrees bearing, about 20 ft step-down, and 3 to 6 plane widths of spacing.
Lead is limited to no more than 120 degrees AOB and no less than 1G.
Wing uses lead, lag, and pure pursuit plus lift-vector placement to stay in the cruise cone.
Minor turns may need small power corrections; aggressive turns should be solved primarily with pursuit geometry.
Lead or Wing calls terminate.
Lead rolls level or establishes a predictable 30-degree AOB turn, stabilizes near 200 KIAS, and clears Wing to parade.
Wing maintains cruise spacing, anticipates acceleration or deceleration, and rejoins without losing step-down.

items.text: The principle of lead is to create a safe, predictable training platform while still meeting mission and area requirements.

children.text: Lead makes smooth, stable, predictable changes in power, heading, and altitude.
Lead keeps the flight within the assigned area and complies with current course rules or clearances.
Lead maintains cloud and traffic clearance unless operating on an IFR clearance.
Lead always knows Wing's position and monitors Wing's energy, aspect, range, closure, heading crossing angle, and line of sight.
Formation tasks take longer than single-ship tasks, so Lead must plan turns, radio changes, checks, and rejoins early.
Lead must understand area boundaries, wind effects, and how maneuver combinations affect ground track.
Lead should manage sun position and avoid forcing Wing to stare through Lead into the sun when practical.
A tight, abrupt maneuver has little training value if Wing cannot safely maintain position.

items.text: Lag and pure pursuit describe where Wing points the nose relative to Lead's flight path, which controls spacing and closure.

children.text: Lead pursuit points the nose ahead of Lead's flight path and decreases nose-to-tail separation.
Pure pursuit points the nose at Lead and shows little or no line-of-sight movement; closure initially exists but reduces as fuselages align.
Lag pursuit points the nose behind Lead's flight path and maintains or increases nose-to-tail separation.
In cruise maneuvering, Wing uses short lead or lag corrections, then returns toward the 60-degree bearing line.
Do not camp at Lead's 6 o'clock; closure is difficult to judge there.
In vertical maneuvering, standard cruise checkpoints may disappear, so preserving step-down is critical.
Supplement technique: compare the inboard horizontal-stabilizer tip to the fuselage star; stab tip on star is pure, stab tip forward of star is lag, and star forward of stab is lead.

studyNotes.summary: F4104 is a formation support and maneuvering event: inspect gear only with disciplined risk control, stop training correctly, and use pursuit geometry to manage cruise maneuvering.

events.overview: F4290 is the formation check event, so the discussion should be cumulative without becoming a memory dump. Be ready to brief the maneuver contracts, safety stop criteria, formation emergency roles, and the method used to review applicable emergency procedures and N/W/Cs.

notes: Adjust specifics to match the assigned profile, weather, and local procedures.
Because the blocks are shared, one edit updates every event that references the same procedure or comm call.
scriptTemplate.title: F4290 Script

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Treat any previously discussed maneuver as a review of contracts, checkpoints, and discontinue criteria rather than a list of isolated steps.

children.text: For departure work, review lineup, interval takeoff, section takeoff, initial rendezvous, and abort responsibilities.
For parade work, review A-B-C corrections, parade turns into and away, crossunder, breakup and rendezvous, underrun, and lead change.
For recovery work, review cruise-to-parade transition, speed brake coordination, section approaches, break spacing, NORDO recovery, and section missed approach.
For cruise maneuvering, review 60-degree bearing, step-down, lead/lag/pure pursuit, terminate, and knock-it-off criteria.
Brief the setup, the visual references, the correction priority, and the common unsafe trend for each maneuver.
Know which aircraft owns deconfliction at each point and when Lead must be directive.
Use terminate for expected training stops, knock-it-off for safety concerns, and underrun when a rendezvous geometry is unsafe.

items.text: Any emergency procedure means the student must show a repeatable review method, not invent an exhaustive list during the brief.

children.text: Start with aircraft control and the applicable NATOPS critical action or checklist.
Add the N/W/Cs that change the decision, timing, or crew coordination.
State whether the emergency is handled as individual aircraft, section support, lost sight, blind, NORDO, Section PEL, airborne damaged aircraft, or down-aircraft response.
Preserve formation separation before trying to preserve flight integrity.
Aviate: maintain aircraft control and execute the correct emergency procedure.
Communicate: use the correct aircraft call sign when one aircraft has the emergency, then be directive on tactical and ATC frequencies.
Separate: transfer lead, move to perch, detach, climb, turn away, or establish altitude separation as the emergency requires.
Recover: choose a suitable field or pattern, coordinate support, and avoid rejoining damaged aircraft unless specifically directed and safe.

events.overview: CS2101 is the advanced-formation capstone sim for dynamic cruise work and formation contingency support. Be ready to brief pursuit geometry, the stop-training calls, formation abort logic, Section PEL responsibilities, and the section approach contract without turning the event into a tail-chase or local-profile dump.

notes: Adjust specifics to match the assigned profile, weather, and local procedures.
Because the blocks are shared, one edit updates every event that references the same procedure or comm call.
scriptTemplate.title: CS2101 Script

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Cruise maneuvering teaches Wing to maintain position with pursuit geometry and lift-vector placement while Lead provides a smooth, predictable maneuvering platform.

children.text: Lead passes the cruise signal and holds a stable platform until Wing is established.
Wing acknowledges, slides to the 60-degree bearing line, sets the directed power, and calls ready.
Formation references use about 80% torque above 10,000 ft and 70% torque below 10,000 ft before maneuvering; hold the PCL position instead of chasing every torque change.
Cruise position is built around the 60-degree bearing line, safe step-down, and enough range to maneuver without drifting through Lead's 6 o'clock.
Local Capstone source cues the scan as altitude, bearing, then closure: exhaust stack tangent to Lead's wing leading edge, ventral fin over the inboard aileron cutout, and pitot tube on the prop arc.
Lead may use level turns and vertical wingovers; the local supplement frames the work as basic level turns followed by vertical maneuvering.
Lead remains within safe maneuvering limits, including no more than 120 degrees AOB and no less than 1G.
Lead should let Wing stabilize before maneuvering and should start with predictable, wingman-considerate turns.
Wing should keep Lead above the canopy rail during vertical work and avoid using PCL as the primary correction for geometry errors.
Terminate or knock-it-off early if closure, step-down, sun, blind geometry, or energy state becomes unsafe.

items.text: Lead, lag, and pure pursuit describe where Wing points the nose relative to Lead's flight path, which controls closure and nose-to-tail spacing.

children.text: Lead pursuit points ahead of Lead's flight path and decreases nose-to-tail separation.
Pure pursuit points at Lead; line-of-sight movement is minimal, and closure decreases as fuselages align.
Lag pursuit points behind Lead's flight path and maintains or increases separation.
In level turns into Wing, Wing tends to become acute and usually needs lag pursuit, bank, and G to realign.
In turns away from Wing, Wing tends to become sucked and uses lead pursuit to regain the bearing line.
In vertical maneuvering, preserve step-down first; exaggerated pursuit curves can create heading crossing angle, blind geometry, or excessive closure.
Supplement technique: horizontal-stabilizer tip on the fuselage star is pure, stab tip forward of the star is lag, and star forward of the stab is lead.

items.text: Knock-it-off and terminate both stop maneuvering, but they communicate different urgency.

children.text: Knock-it-off is for safety-of-flight issues such as emergency, traffic conflict, blind situation, G-LOC or AGSM failure, area boundary, or any unsafe trend.
Any flight member may call it and should state the reason if able.
After the call, Lead maneuvers predictably, gives directive intentions, and may add altitude and reference heading.
Terminate is an expected or administrative stop: learning objective complete, maneuver complete, or Wing needs to stop the exercise without a safety emergency.
Lead normally initiates terminate, but Wing may request or initiate it.
Lead transitions to a safe attitude, directs follow-on intentions, and clears Wing back to parade or another briefed position when stable.

items.text: An aborted takeoff in formation is a separation problem as much as an aircraft problem. Decide, stay on the assigned side, and communicate when aircraft control permits.

children.text: Brief abort contingencies before takeoff.
If aborting, execute the NATOPS abort procedure, maintain directional control, remain on the assigned runway side, and transmit intentions.
If Lead aborts during an interval takeoff, Wing normally aborts behind Lead while maintaining Wing's side; the interval should provide spacing.
If Wing aborts during an interval takeoff, Wing aborts on Wing's side and transmits once Lead is airborne and Wing is under control.
If either aircraft aborts after section brake release, the aborting aircraft stays on its side and executes the abort.

The non-aborting aircraft recognizes the rapid line-of-sight change, selects maximum power, maintains runway-side discipline, and continues as an individual takeoff unless separation cannot be maintained or it has its own emergency.
Wing must be prepared to avoid Lead if Lead loses directional control, including changing sides or leaving the prepared surface if required to prevent collision.

items.text: A Section PEL gives the emergency aircraft the maneuvering room and authority it needs while preserving mutual support.

children.text: If Lead has the emergency, Lead should make a quick radio call so Wing can get separation.
If Wing has the emergency, Wing requests lead left or right.
Lead transfers lead verbally only after visual contact and separation make the transfer safe.
The new Wing transitions to perch and supports the emergency aircraft.
Wing clears the flight path, provides divert or field information, assists with procedures if requested, and monitors altitude, airspeed, VSI, and configuration.
The emergency aircraft maneuvers and configures for high key; Wing matches configuration if remaining through the profile.
Lead may kiss off Wing at any time.
If Wing remains through the ELP, Wing stays outside Lead's turn and waves off when directed, no lower than 300 ft AGL.
Normally, Wing can safely detach and monitor at high key.

items.text: A section approach is a mutual-support recovery that requires Lead to fly a smooth approach and Wing to maintain visual contact, configuration awareness, and readiness to assume Lead.

children.text: Plan the approach, missed approach, configuration timing, and final separation before starting down the approach.
Weather must be at or above circling minimums, or 1000 ft and 3 SM if circling minimums are not published.
Bring Wing to parade, reduce airspeed, and configure the flight no later than the FAF; earlier may be needed in IMC or VFR on top.
Confirm configuration with a clear visual or radio response.
Lead positions the formation on final and normally flies 120 KIAS with Wing in parade until detached.
Wing mirrors Lead's configuration, maintains visual contact in IMC, and stays ready to assume Lead.
If the section misses approach, execute the published missed approach using normal hand signals or tactical frequency unless otherwise briefed.
If individual approaches are required, Lead coordinates separate squawks and normally sends the lower-fuel aircraft first.
Use current local SOP, IFG, and day-of brief for field-specific detach or landing-flow details.

events.overview: CS2102 completes the advanced-formation sim pair by focusing on separation and rejoin contracts: formation aborts, dissolving the flight, radial rendezvous, and fan-break recovery. The student should brief each procedure as a deconfliction problem first and a formation technique second.

notes: Adjust specifics to match the assigned profile, weather, and local procedures.
Because the blocks are shared, one edit updates every event that references the same procedure or comm call.
scriptTemplate.title: CS2102 Script

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: An aborted takeoff in formation is first about maintaining aircraft control and preserving lateral separation.

children.text: Brief abort responsibilities before takeoff; do not let the first discussion happen after brake release.
If aborting, execute the NATOPS abort procedure, maintain directional control, stay on the assigned runway side, and transmit intentions when able.
If Lead aborts during an interval takeoff, Wing normally aborts behind Lead while maintaining Wing's runway side.
If Wing aborts during an interval takeoff, Wing aborts on Wing's side and transmits once Lead is safely airborne and Wing is under control.
If either aircraft aborts after section brake release, the aborting aircraft remains on its side and executes the abort.

The non-aborting aircraft recognizes the rapid line-of-sight rate, selects maximum power, maintains its runway side, and executes an individual takeoff unless separation cannot be maintained or it has its own emergency.
Wing must be ready to avoid Lead if Lead loses directional control, including changing runway sides or leaving the prepared surface if that is required to prevent collision.

items.text: Dissolving the flight turns a formation into individual aircraft while preserving positive separation, ATC coordination, and clear responsibility.

children.text: Complete required formation training and any needed lead change before the split.
Lead assigns heading and altitude separation; local event source uses at least 30 degrees of heading separation and normally 500 ft of altitude separation.
Wing normally turns away and descends to the assigned heading and altitude.
Lead maintains the original altitude until Wing reports established.
Use clear readbacks for heading, altitude, area, and detach clearance.
Wing sets the appropriate transponder or TCAS configuration per the brief and current local procedure.
Lead coordinates with ATC when the flight is splitting and dissolves the formation only after aircraft are established in their assigned blocks or areas.
For later rejoin, Wing reports ready on the tactical frequency and Lead coordinates the join clearance.
Keep local area names, frequencies, and route-specific calls tied to the day-of brief, not memorized as universal procedure.

items.text: Radial rendezvous is a structured blind or visual circular rendezvous that lets a separated flight rejoin using a known fix, altitude block, airspeed, and turn direction.

children.text: Lead establishes the rendezvous circle tangent to the briefed fix and flies the briefed direction.
Lead uses about 30 degrees AOB, maintains altitude and 200 KIAS, and calls position points at each 90-degree interval until Wing reports visual.
Lead adjusts for wind so point one remains tied to the fix.
Wing proceeds toward the point-one fix 500 ft below the briefed rendezvous altitude.
Wing remains 500 ft low until established on Lead's bearing line with fuselage alignment.
At point one, or another known circle point, Wing initiates the briefed turn direction even if Lead is not yet in sight.
Wing responds to Lead's position calls with DME or other briefed position awareness until visual.
After visual, Wing calls visual, climbs to Lead's altitude by placing Lead on the horizon, and completes the standard join-up.
If sight picture or situational awareness supports it, Wing may use the center of the circle as a control zone before beginning lead/lag maneuvering.
Do not rush from blind geometry into a high-closure join; preserve altitude separation until the visual rejoin is stable.

items.text: The fan break is a formation pattern-entry tool that creates interval through matched roll rate plus predictable power and speed-brake differences.

children.text: Lead initiates with the follow-me signal.
Lead smoothly rolls to about 45 degrees AOB at a rate Wing can match.
Lead normally holds power through about 90 degrees of turn, then retards the PCL to idle.
Lead makes required landing-pattern calls for the flight.
Wing matches Lead's roll rate.
Wing retards the PCL to idle and extends speed brake at maneuver start to build spacing.
Wing reports gear-down status after Lead's clearance-to-land call according to current SOP or course rules.
After landing, rejoin as a flight only after crossing the hold-short line and taxiing back together as briefed.
The maneuver depends on predictable timing; abrupt roll, late speed brake, or mismatched power can collapse spacing.
Use current local course rules for field-specific pattern calls and runway flow.

studyNotes.summary: CS2102 should be studied as a formation separation-and-rejoin event: abort safely, split the flight deliberately, rejoin with a structured radial rendezvous, and use fan-break spacing without improvising local calls.

events.overview: CS3101 reintroduces familiarization maneuvers, then moves the student into the IFR environment with an IFR pick-up and GCA pattern. The discussion should show that basic aircraft-control habits, radio discipline, and instrument scan still work when the profile shifts from FAM-style airwork to radar-controlled approaches.

notes: Adjust specifics to match the assigned profile, weather, and local procedures.
Because the blocks are shared, one edit updates every event that references the same procedure or comm call.
scriptTemplate.title: CS3101 Script

sourceDocuments.summary: Source document tied to this event.
sourceDocuments.title: CS3101

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Treat the familiarization review as a scan-and-control refresh, not a complete re-teaching of every prior FAM event.

children.text: Be ready to brief G-warm, aerobatics, stalls, spin, unusual-attitude recovery, landing profiles, waveoff, ELP, and holding or approach setup at the level already learned.
For each maneuver, start with purpose, setup, safety boundary, execution, completion cue, and the common error that usually starts the debrief.
Keep checklist, clear-area, trim, coordination, and energy management in every answer.
The sim objective is to rebuild cross-check and aircraft control, then transition smoothly to IFR work.
Do not let the FAM maneuver review consume the IFR brief; prioritize the maneuvers most likely to affect instrument transition, approach work, and recovery judgment.

items.text: An IFR pick-up converts the flight into the IFR system; the radio call must give ATC enough information to identify the aircraft, build the clearance, and understand fuel and alternate context.

children.text: Aircraft identification.
Position and time.
Route, altitude, and destination.
True airspeed in knots.
ETE from the point of change to destination and hours of fuel remaining.
Alternate airport.
Name, rank, and honors code of VIP aboard if the destination is being changed.
Build the call from the current flight state; do not recite a canned local route if the aircraft position, destination, or fuel state has changed.
Keep the aircraft under control and trimmed before starting the clearance conversation.
Read back the clearance precisely and verify route, altitude, transponder, and lost-comm expectations before leaving VFR assumptions behind.

items.text: The GCA pattern is a radar-approach control exercise: fly precise headings, airspeeds, configuration changes, descents, and missed-approach cleanup while the controller or instructor drives small corrections.

children.text: Start clean at 200 KIAS on a cardinal heading at base altitude.
Use standard-rate turns, not more than 30 degrees AOB, and lead rollouts with the one-third rule.
Slow to 150 KIAS using about 15% torque, then stabilize near 33% torque once level at 150 KIAS.
Expect radar-style calls such as standby for the turn, maintain, and clear call when being turned to final approach course.
Transition to BAC by reducing power to about 15%, lowering gear and T/O flaps below 150 KIAS, and executing the Before Landing Checklist.
Trim for 120 KIAS; local event gouge uses about 42% torque to stabilize level at 120 KIAS before the descent.
For the simulated GCA descent, use about 24% torque and a nose-low attitude to hold 120 KIAS and roughly 600 FPM.
Expect small heading corrections, often about 3 to 10 degrees, while maintaining airspeed, descent rate, and assigned headings.
After the planned descent segment, execute the missed approach: maximum power, right rudder, and about 10 to 15 degrees nose high.
Confirm two positive rates with VSI and altimeter before raising the gear.
Above 110 KIAS, raise flaps; report gear and flaps up before 150 KIAS.
Set about 8 to 10 degrees nose high, climb at 180 KIAS for the assigned climb segment, then transition back to 200 KIAS cruise before level-off.
Common errors are poor nose-power coordination in descent, over-rotating during the missed approach, delayed gear or flap retraction, and poor rudder trim causing heading drift.

events.overview: CS3102 is the advanced IMC emergency capstone sim. It expects the student to connect familiarization review, IMC emergency judgment, and lost-communications rules while still flying the aircraft, managing task saturation, and choosing the safest recovery path.

notes: Adjust specifics to match the assigned profile, weather, and local procedures.
Because the blocks are shared, one edit updates every event that references the same procedure or comm call.
scriptTemplate.title: CS3102 Script

sourceDocuments.summary: Source document tied to this event.
sourceDocuments.title: CS3102

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Use the familiarization review to prove the basics still hold when the sim adds weather, approaches, emergencies, and communications failure.

children.text: Be ready for G-warm, aerobatics, stalls, spin, unusual-attitude recovery, landing profiles, waveoff, ELP, and instrument approach transitions.
For each prior FAM item, brief purpose, setup, safety boundary, recovery cue, and the most likely error.
Keep trim, coordination, checklist discipline, and energy management connected to the instrument task that follows.
The event source introduces total communications failure during radar vectors to final in IMC, so review FAM maneuvers with enough organization left over for IFR emergency decision making.
Do not answer with a local-only route or canned profile; use current weather, fuel, clearance, approach status, and aircraft condition.

items.text: IMC emergencies are judgment problems first: maintain aircraft control, analyze the situation, take proper action, and land as soon as conditions require.

children.text: Maintain aircraft control and establish a reliable instrument scan before troubleshooting.
Execute required critical action memory items immediately, then use the checklist when time and aircraft control permit.
Use CRM inside and outside the cockpit: divide tasks, talk to ATC, and ask for vectors or priority handling when needed.
Modify procedures as required for multiple emergencies, terrain, weather, fuel, or aircraft-control limits.
For inadvertent IMC, spatial disorientation, malfunction, or IMC abort, climb immediately to the applicable emergency route altitude or safe altitude.
Squawk 7700 if declaring an emergency or unable to communicate normally.
Notify ATC of intentions when able and request vectors to a suitable field if that is the safest plan.
If already on an IFR clearance, do not deviate from clearance or route without ATC coordination unless emergency authority is required.
NATOPS and procedural references support judgment; they do not replace it.
Do not let communications, navigation, or checklist work pull the scan away from attitude, altitude, airspeed, and terrain clearance.

items.text: Lost communications in IFR conditions requires a disciplined plan, but pilot judgment still determines whether the situation has become an emergency.

children.text: If radio failure occurs in VMC, or VMC is encountered after the failure, continue under VFR and land as soon as practicable at a suitable field.
Land as soon as practicable is not the same as land immediately; do not choose an unsuitable or unauthorized field just to end the radio problem.
Fly the last route assigned in an ATC clearance.
If being radar vectored, proceed direct to the fix, route, or airway specified in the vector clearance.
If no assigned route applies, fly the route ATC advised to expect.
If none of those exist, fly the filed flight-plan route.
For each route segment, fly the highest of assigned altitude, minimum IFR altitude, or expected altitude.
If an expect-further-climb altitude was issued, maintain assigned or minimum altitude until the expected time or fix, then climb as cleared by the lost-comm rule set.
Comply with MEA, MCA, and MRA requirements as the route changes.
If the clearance limit is an IAF, begin descent and approach as close as possible to the EFC time, or ETA if no EFC was received.
If the clearance limit is not an IAF, leave at the EFC time if received, or upon arrival if no EFC was received, then proceed to an IAF and begin descent or approach as close as possible to ETA.
Squawk 7600 for radio failure unless emergency authority requires a different code.
Attempt contact on the last assigned frequency, available FSS or controlling agencies, and 121.5 if available.
When contact is restored, give position, altitude, last assigned frequency, and request further clearance.
ATC may assume lost-comm compliance, but the pilot may deviate under emergency authority when circumstances demand it.

events.overview: CS4101 is the first Capstone maneuver-and-EP flight. The discussion should show that the student can brief prior maneuvers by setup, contract, and discontinue criteria, then apply emergency procedures with N/W/C judgment and a practical recovery plan.

notes: Adjust specifics to match the assigned profile, weather, and local procedures.
Because the blocks are shared, one edit updates every event that references the same procedure or comm call.
scriptTemplate.title: CS4101 Script

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Any previously discussed maneuver means the instructor can sample across FAM, Formation, Instrument, and VNAV-style skills; answer with an organized method instead of trying to recite the whole syllabus.

children.text: Start with the maneuver purpose, entry setup, configuration, airspeed, altitude or area requirement, and clear-area or formation contract.
State the execution flow, maneuver-complete cue, and the reason you would discontinue, terminate, or knock-it-off.
Connect the maneuver to the capstone profile: formation work, high work, instrument approach, missed approach, holding, divert, or recovery.
For FAM maneuvers, keep trim, coordination, stall/OCF awareness, energy state, and recovery altitude in the answer.
For formation maneuvers, brief who owns deconfliction, what visual reference matters, and when Wing must call lost sight, blind, terminate, or knock-it-off.
For instrument work, brief setup, clearance or route logic, scan priorities, configuration timing, missed-approach plan, and lost-comm assumptions.
For navigation or VNAV-style tasks, brief route verification, fuel/time awareness, weather, airspace, and how the plan changes if the profile no longer matches the day.
Do not memorize local profile names as the procedure. Use current 1801, SOP, IFG, weather, fuel, and day-of brief to decide which procedure applies.
If a maneuver answer depends on local routing, frequency, runway flow, or holding fix, say that it must be verified from the current local source.

items.text: Any emergency procedure means the student must show a repeatable decision flow: cue, aircraft control, memory item, checklist or N/W/C, and recovery choice.

children.text: Aviate first: maintain control, establish the correct attitude and airspeed, and protect altitude, terrain clearance, and formation separation.
Analyze the cue and execute any required critical action memory items.
Use the checklist and N/W/Cs to decide whether the branch is continue, recover, PEL, forced landing, section support, divert, or eject.
Communicate intentions to the other aircraft, ATC, or support agency when the aircraft is stable enough.
For single-ship EPs, brief recognition, immediate actions, minimum controllable or glide numbers, and the field or ejection decision point.
For formation EPs, brief lead transfer, perch, detach, lost sight or blind separation, and who coordinates with ATC.
For IMC EPs, prioritize instrument scan, safe altitude, clearance or emergency authority, and lost-comm plan.
For divert or damaged-aircraft cases, brief suitable field selection, fuel, weather, runway, crash crew, and whether the flight should remain joined.
Do not invent an exhaustive EP list for the event. Use the published EP/N/W/C source for verbatim items and be ready to apply them to the profile.
When the emergency conflicts with the original mission plan, the recovery plan wins.

events.overview: CS4102 is the second Capstone maneuver-and-EP flight. The brief should sound less like a first exposure and more like mission management: select the right prior maneuver method, adapt to weather or routing changes, and apply emergency procedures without losing fuel, clearance, or recovery awareness.

notes: Adjust specifics to match the assigned profile, weather, and local procedures.
Because the blocks are shared, one edit updates every event that references the same procedure or comm call.
scriptTemplate.title: CS4102 Script

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Any previously discussed maneuver on CS4102 is a readiness check across the whole primary syllabus, with the added expectation that the student can adapt when the plan changes.

children.text: Brief the planned maneuver by purpose, entry setup, execution, completion cue, and discontinue or reset criteria.
Add the operational context: current area, airspace, weather, fuel, formation status, clearance, and recovery plan.
If the instructor changes the profile, rebuild the setup deliberately instead of carrying old altitude, airspeed, configuration, or clearance assumptions forward.
For contact work, focus on energy management, trim, coordination, stall or OCF cues, ELP judgment, and recovery altitude.
For formation work, focus on sight, step-down, deconfliction, lead transfer, section approach, flight split, rejoin, and stop-training calls.
For instrument work, focus on clearance limits, approach setup, missed approach, holding, lost-comm logic, and backup navigation.
For navigation work, focus on route verification, fuel, weather, airspace, divert suitability, and whether the plan still meets the sortie objective.
A capstone answer should say what changes the decision: deteriorating weather, lower fuel, a different approach, a lost display, a section emergency, or an unplanned hold.
Use current 1801, SOP, IFG, route packet, weather, and day-of brief for local details; keep the reusable note focused on the decision method.

items.text: Any emergency procedure on CS4102 should be briefed as a mission-management branch: stabilize the aircraft, execute the correct EP, then decide whether to continue, recover, divert, support the section, or eject.

children.text: Identify the cue and protect aircraft control before troubleshooting.
Execute memory items and then back them up with the checklist when time permits.
Apply the N/W/Cs that change the branch, especially altitude, airspeed, configuration, weather, and formation-separation limits.
Communicate the plan once the aircraft is stable enough: other aircraft, ATC, tower, or support agency as appropriate.
If the EP affects controllability or engine reliability, brief the PEL, forced-landing, or ejection boundary instead of trying to preserve the original profile.
If the EP occurs in formation, brief lead transfer, perch, detach, section support, lost sight or blind separation, and whether the flight should remain joined.
If the EP occurs in IMC, brief safe altitude, clearance or emergency authority, lost-comm implications, and nearest suitable recovery.
If the EP drives a divert, brief field suitability, runway, weather, fuel, crash crew, and whether a formation or individual recovery is safer.
Do not turn 'any EP' into a guessed list. Use the applicable EP and N/W/C source for verbatim items, then show the decision tree that follows.
A mature answer states when the original mission is over and the emergency recovery plan has priority.

items.text: Any Previously Discussed Maneuver and Any Emergency Procedure

events.overview: CS4290 is the Capstone check flight. The discussion should prove the student can brief any prior maneuver and any emergency procedure as an integrated mission problem, then adapt to real-time contingencies without inventing procedures or losing the recovery picture.

notes: Adjust specifics to match the assigned profile, weather, and local procedures.
Because the blocks are shared, one edit updates every event that references the same procedure or comm call.
scriptTemplate.title: CS4290 Script

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Any previously discussed maneuver on the check flight is not a request to dump every prior event. It is a prompt to show a repeatable brief format and apply the right procedure to the actual scenario.

children.text: State the maneuver purpose, entry setup, airspeed, altitude or area requirement, configuration, and clearance or formation contract.
Brief execution, completion cue, common error, and the condition that requires reset, terminate, knock-it-off, missed approach, or recovery.
Tie the maneuver to the profile: formation departure or rejoin, high work, instrument approach, missed approach, holding, divert, or recovery.
Formation scenario: depart on separate clearances, rejoin in the working area, conduct radial rendezvous, split or rejoin the flight, or manage a section emergency.
Instrument scenario: fly a published missed approach, accept a different approach after ATIS, handle unplanned holding, or navigate point-to-point.
Navigation scenario: fly a leg without the TSD when airspace and flight plan permit, using backup navigation and cross-checks.
Weather or fuel scenario: recognize when simulated weather, divert suitability, holding, fuel, or approach changes should replace the original plan.
Use current 1801, route packet, SOP, IFG, weather, fuel, NOTAMs, and day-of brief for local execution details.
A strong answer explains how the plan changes, who needs to be told, and what must be verified before continuing.

items.text: Any emergency procedure on CS4290 is a check of recognition, memory items, N/W/C interpretation, and recovery judgment, not a challenge to invent a list of emergencies.

children.text: Cue: identify the malfunction or emergency from indications, aircraft behavior, environment, or formation context.
Control: protect aircraft attitude, airspeed, altitude, terrain clearance, and formation separation.
Action: execute required memory items, then use the checklist and N/W/Cs to choose the correct branch.
Recover: decide whether to continue, divert, PEL, forced-land, fly a missed approach, coordinate section support, or eject.
For a single-aircraft emergency, state the aircraft-control target, memory item, checklist/N/W/C, field or ejection decision, and radio plan.
For a section emergency, state lead transfer, perch, detach, lost sight or blind separation, and who coordinates with ATC or tower.
For IMC or approach emergencies, state safe altitude, clearance or emergency authority, lost-communications assumptions, missed approach, and suitable recovery field.
For weather divert or damaged-aircraft cases, state field suitability, runway, fuel, crash crew, approach options, and whether the flight should remain joined.
Do not brief a scenario-specific contingency as universal procedure unless the controlling source says so.
When the emergency creates a conflict with the planned check-flight profile, the emergency recovery plan takes priority.
